sources: P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED - READ AT SOURCE: STCW Convention, regulation VIII/1 (Fitness for duty), STCW Consolidated Edition 2017, MIW True Source corpus. Paragraph 1 requires each Administration, for the purpose of preventing fatigue, to (.1) establish and enforce rest periods for watchkeeping personnel and those whose duties involve designated safety, security and prevention of pollution duties in accordance with section A-VIII/1, and (.2) require that watch systems are so arranged that the efficiency of all watchkeeping personnel is not impaired by fatigue and that duties are so organized that the first watch at the commencement of a voyage and subsequent relieving watches are sufficiently rested and otherwise fit for duty. Paragraph 2 requires adequate measures against drug and alcohol abuse in accordance with section A-VIII/1, taking into account the guidance in section B-VIII/1.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED - READ AT SOURCE: STCW Code section A-VIII/1, paragraphs 1 to 3. Administrations shall take account of the danger posed by fatigue. Persons assigned duty as officer in charge of a watch or as a rating forming part of a watch, and those whose duties involve designated safety, prevention of pollution and security duties, shall be provided with a rest period of not less than 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period. The hours of rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive periods of rest shall not exceed 14 hours.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED - READ AT SOURCE: STCW Code section A-VIII/1, paragraph 4. The rest requirements in paragraphs 2 and 3 need not be maintained in the case of an emergency or in other overriding operational conditions. Musters, fire-fighting and lifeboat drills, and drills prescribed by national laws and regulations and by international instruments, shall be conducted in a manner that minimizes the disturbance of rest periods and does not induce fatigue.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED - READ AT SOURCE: STCW Code section A-VIII/1, paragraphs 5 to 7. Watch schedules shall be posted where they are easily accessible, established in a standardized format in the working language or languages of the ship and in English. A seafarer on call, such as when a machinery space is unattended, shall have an adequate compensatory rest period if the normal period of rest is disturbed by call-outs to work. Records of daily hours of rest shall be maintained in a standardized format, in the working language or languages of the ship and in English, to allow monitoring and verification; seafarers shall receive a copy of the records pertaining to them, endorsed by the master or a person authorized by the master and by the seafarers.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED - READ AT SOURCE: STCW Code section A-VIII/1, paragraph 8 - the master's authority. Nothing in the section impairs the right of the master to require a seafarer to perform any hours of work necessary for the immediate safety of the ship, persons on board or cargo, or for the purpose of giving assistance to other ships or persons in distress at sea. The master may suspend the schedule of hours of rest and require a seafarer to perform any hours of work necessary until the normal situation has been restored; as soon as practicable after the normal situation has been restored, the master shall ensure that any seafarers who have performed work in a scheduled rest period are provided with an adequate period of rest.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED - READ AT SOURCE: STCW Code section A-VIII/1, paragraph 9 - the exceptions regime. Parties may allow exceptions from the required hours of rest in paragraphs 2.2 and 3 provided that the rest period is not less than 70 hours in any 7-day period. Exceptions from the weekly rest period shall not be allowed for more than two consecutive weeks, and the intervals between two periods of exceptions on board shall not be less than twice the duration of the exception. The hours of rest in paragraph 2.1 may be divided into no more than three periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours and neither of the other two less than one hour, with intervals between consecutive periods of rest not exceeding 14 hours, and exceptions shall not extend beyond two 24-hour periods in any 7-day period. Exceptions shall as far as possible take into account the guidance on prevention of fatigue in section B-VIII/1.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED - READ AT SOURCE: STCW Code section A-VIII/1, paragraph 10 - the alcohol limit. Each Administration shall establish, for the purpose of preventing alcohol abuse, a limit of not greater than 0.05% blood alcohol level (BAC) or 0.25 mg/l alcohol in the breath, or a quantity of alcohol leading to such alcohol concentration, for masters, officers and other seafarers while performing designated safety, security and marine environmental duties.

blocks.h: 1. What Chapter VIII requires, and where the criteria are written

blocks.p: Chapter VIII of the STCW Convention is headed Watchkeeping and contains two regulations. Regulation VIII/1, 'Fitness for duty', is the one this question asks about. It is short, and it is a duty on the Administration rather than a set of numbers: for the purpose of preventing fatigue, each Administration must (i) establish and enforce rest periods for watchkeeping personnel and for those whose duties involve designated safety, security and prevention of pollution duties, in accordance with section A-VIII/1; and (ii) require that watch systems are so arranged that the efficiency of watchkeeping personnel is not impaired by fatigue, and that the first watch at the commencement of a voyage and subsequent relieving watches are sufficiently rested and otherwise fit for duty. Paragraph 2 adds the same duty for drug and alcohol abuse.

The measurable criteria therefore live in the mandatory Code, section A-VIII/1, with non-mandatory guidance in section B-VIII/1. Note who is covered: not only the watch, but anyone with designated safety, pollution-prevention or security duties.

blocks.h: 2. Criterion one - the minimum hours of rest

ul: Not less than 10 hours of rest in any 24-hour period; and
77 hours of rest in any 7-day period.
The criterion is expressed as rest, not as hours of work, and it is a rolling measure - any 24 hours and any 7 days, not the calendar day or the calendar week.

blocks.h: 3. Criterion two - how that rest may be broken up

blocks.p: Hours are worthless if they are shredded, so the Code controls the shape of the rest as well as its quantity. Rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which must be at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive periods of rest must not exceed 14 hours. The 6-hour block is what protects a consolidated sleep; the 14-hour ceiling is what stops a long unbroken stretch of duty.

A Party may allow exceptions, but they are themselves bounded: rest must still be not less than 70 hours in any 7-day period; rest may then be split into no more than three periods, one of at least 6 hours and neither of the others less than one hour; the 14-hour interval still applies; exceptions may not extend beyond two 24-hour periods in any 7-day period, may not run for more than two consecutive weeks, and must be separated by an interval of at least twice the duration of the exception.

Each Administration must establish a limit of not greater than 0.05% blood alcohol level, or 0.25 mg/l alcohol in the breath, for masters, officers and other seafarers while performing designated safety, security and marine environmental duties. This is a fitness criterion in the literal sense - a threshold of impairment - and it is enforced through company drug and alcohol policy, unannounced testing and port State inspection.

blocks.h: 5. Criterion four - the administrative criteria that make the rest rules real

ul: Watch schedules shall be posted where easily accessible, in a standardized format, in the working language of the ship and in English.

Records of daily hours of rest shall be maintained in the same standardized format and languages, so that compliance can be monitored and verified; the seafarer receives a copy, endorsed by the master or an authorized person and by the seafarer.
A seafarer on call - the standing case of an unattended machinery space - must be given adequate compensatory rest if the normal rest period is disturbed by call-outs.
Drills must be conducted so as to minimize the disturbance of rest periods and not induce fatigue.

blocks.h: 6. The master's overriding authority, and what follows it

blocks.p: The rest requirements need not be maintained in an emergency or in other overriding operational conditions, and nothing in the section impairs the master's right to require any hours of work necessary for the immediate safety of the ship, persons on board or cargo, or to assist others in distress. The master may suspend the schedule until the normal situation is restored. The provision is not a loophole, because it carries its own closing obligation: as soon as practicable afterwards the master must ensure that anyone who worked during scheduled rest is given an adequate period of rest.

blocks.h: 7. How these criteria produce a safe and effective watch

blocks.p: They work as a system rather than as a list. Fatigue degrades exactly what a watch is for - vigilance, reaction time, judgement and the ability to detect a slow-developing abnormality - and it does so without the sufferer noticing, which is why a subjective 'fit to stand a watch' test is useless and a quantified, recorded one is not. The quantity rule sets a floor; the division rule ensures the floor is usable sleep rather than scattered fragments; the alcohol limit removes a second impairment that would compound the first; the posted schedule turns compliance into something that must be planned in advance, which is what forces adequate manning rather than heroic individuals; the records make it auditable by the flag State, by port State control and by the company's own ISM system; and the master's override, bounded by compensating rest, keeps the regime credible in a real emergency instead of inviting routine falsification. Regulation VIII/1.1.2 completes the loop by making the relieving watch the test: a watch system is compliant only if the officer who takes over is genuinely rested and fit for duty.

The stem is two questions joined by 'How'. The first - the criteria - is concrete and is marked by counting: the numbers, the division rule, the exceptions, the alcohol limit, the schedules and the records. The second - how they ensure safe and effective watchkeeping - is the discussion mark, and it is the half most candidates omit. Steps 2 to 6 bank the concrete marks; step 7 exists solely to answer the second half of the question, and without it a technically perfect list of numbers is only half an answer.

Note also where the criteria live. The question says 'as outlined in STCW Chapter 8', but regulation VIII/1 contains almost no detail - it delegates to section A-VIII/1 of the Code. Saying so in one sentence at the start shows the examiner you know how the Convention and Code fit together, and it costs nothing.

Fatigue is an invisible impairment. A tired officer does not feel unfit; he feels normal and performs badly, and the first evidence is usually the incident. Every criterion in section A-VIII/1 is an attempt to control something that cannot be self-assessed, by turning it into something that can be scheduled, measured, recorded and inspected. Once you see that, the structure of the section explains itself: a quantity rule, a shape rule, a chemical-impairment rule, and three administrative rules that make the first three enforceable.

ul: Giving the MLC hours-of-work figures instead of the STCW hours-of-rest figures, or mixing the two frameworks. STCW A-VIII/1 is written as minimum rest: 10 in 24 and 77 in 7.
Quoting 72 hours in 7 days. That is the MLC maximum hours of work. The STCW rest figure is 77.
Giving the 10 and the 77 and stopping. The division rule - two periods, one of at least 6 hours, 14-hour maximum interval - carries marks of its own.
Omitting the exceptions regime entirely, or giving the 70-hour floor without the conditions that fence it.
Restricting the criteria to watchkeepers. They also cover those with designated safety, security and prevention of pollution duties.
Treating the master's override as an unqualified power. It is followed by a mandatory compensating rest obligation.
Forgetting that the records must be in English as well as the working language, and that the seafarer gets a signed copy.
Answering only the first half of the stem and never addressing how the criteria deliver a safe watch.

0.05% BAC and 0.25 mg/l are two expressions of one limit, and the Code says not greater than - an Administration may set a stricter figure, and many companies operate zero tolerance. Do not present 0.05% as an entitlement.
'Any 24-hour period' and 'any 7-day period'. The measure is rolling. A schedule that complies on calendar days can still breach it.
The exception permits three periods, not two - and the two additional periods must each be at least one hour. Candidates routinely give the normal rule and the exception the same shape.
Two consecutive weeks maximum, and the gap afterwards must be at least twice the duration of the exception. That second condition is almost always missed.
The on-call provision is the engineer's provision. An unattended machinery space is the example the Code itself gives, so expect to be asked how you compensate an engineer called out overnight.
Drills are expressly required not to induce fatigue - a favourite follow-up, because it sits at the junction of two safety obligations that appear to conflict.

blocks.h: The sitting date - what was and was not law in September 2024

blocks.p: The operative instrument is the STCW Convention and Code as amended, in the form of the 2017 consolidated edition together with the amendments in force by this date - MSC.416/417(97) from 1 July 2018 and MSC.486/487(103) from 1 January 2023. Section A-VIII/1 itself is unchanged by either.

Two things must not be presented as law at this sitting. MSC.560(108), which makes training on the prevention of harassment, bullying and sexual assault mandatory in table A-VI/1-4, was adopted in 2024 but does not enter into force until 1 January 2026 - and it is Chapter VI, not Chapter VIII. And the comprehensive review of STCW being taken forward through the HTW Sub-Committee was, at this date, work in progress. It is entirely legitimate - and a mark of a management-level answer - to say that fitness for duty and fatigue are among the areas under review, provided it is stated as a transition underway and not as a requirement.

ul: State the minimum hours of rest. Now state them as a maximum working day.
Your second engineer has been called out three times overnight from an unattended machinery space. What do you owe him, and where is that written?
What records do you keep, in what languages, and who signs them?
A port State control officer asks for evidence of compliance. What do you produce?
What is the alcohol limit, and does it apply to you when you are off watch but on call?
The ship is short-handed and you propose to work an exception. What are the limits on that?
You have just come through a heavy-weather emergency and nobody has rested for eighteen hours. What does the Code require of the master now?

blocks.p: Six criteria in the order you will write them: HOW MUCH (2), WHAT SHAPE (3), HOW SOBER (4), ON PAPER (5), WHO MAY BREAK IT (6), WHY IT WORKS (7). For the numbers use the pair 10 and 77 for the normal rule and 70 for the exception floor - the exception figure is lower, which is the direction that makes sense. Then 2 periods / 6 hours / 14-hour interval normally, and 3 periods / 6 hours / 1 hour minimum / 2 days a week / 2 weeks maximum under exception.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: STCW Code section A-VIII/1, made mandatory by regulation VIII/1. Regulation VIII/1 states the objective - preventing fatigue, and preventing drug and alcohol abuse - and delegates every measurable criterion to section A-VIII/1. Quoting the regulation without the Code section gives the examiner the duty but none of the criteria the question asks for.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering with the MLC hours-of-work figures. STCW section A-VIII/1 is written as MINIMUM REST - 10 in 24 and 77 in 7 - not as maximum work, and 77 is not 72. The second trap is giving the two headline numbers and stopping: the division rule, the exceptions regime with its 70-hour floor, the alcohol limit and the records are all part of 'the criteria'. The third is never answering the second half of the stem.

questions.memory_cue: Six criteria in writing order: HOW MUCH (2), WHAT SHAPE (3), HOW SOBER (4), ON PAPER (5), WHO MAY BREAK IT (6), WHY IT WORKS (7). Numbers: 10 and 77 normally, 70 as the exception floor - the exception figure is lower, which is the direction that makes sense.
questions.understand_first: Fatigue is an impairment you cannot feel. A tired watchkeeper does not experience himself as unfit - he experiences himself as normal and performs badly, and the first hard evidence is usually the incident itself. That single fact explains the whole of section A-VIII/1. Because fitness for duty cannot be left to self-assessment, the Convention converts it into something that can be scheduled in advance, measured in hours, written down and inspected by somebody else. So the criteria come in two layers: a quantity of rest and a shape for that rest, which control the fatigue itself; and posted schedules, standardized records and a signed copy for the seafarer, which exist purely so that the first layer can be enforced against a company that would otherwise be tempted to run the ship one person short.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the STCW fitness-for-duty question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Where the criteria live - regulation VIII/1 delegates to Code section A-VIII/1. 2 How much rest. 3 What shape that rest must take, including the exceptions. 4 The alcohol limit. 5 The administrative criteria - schedules, records, compensatory rest. 6 The master's override and the rest that must follow it. 7 How it all produces a safe and effective watch.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 2 to 6 are the criteria the stem asks for; step 7 answers the second half of the stem, which is the half most candidates never reach.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the minimum hours of rest and the rule on how they may be divided.
retrieval_cards.answer: Not less than 10 hours of rest in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period. The hours of rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours in length, and the interval between consecutive periods of rest shall not exceed 14 hours.
retrieval_cards.why: Four numbers, and candidates routinely give only the first two. The rolling wording - any 24 hours, any 7 days - is also marked.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the limits on exceptions from the required hours of rest?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rest must be not less than 70 hours in any 7-day period. Rest may then be divided into no more than three periods, one of at least 6 hours and neither of the other two less than one hour, with intervals not exceeding 14 hours. Exceptions may not extend beyond two 24-hour periods in any 7-day period, may not be allowed for more than two consecutive weeks, and the interval between two periods of exceptions must be at least twice the duration of the exception.
retrieval_cards.why: The exceptions regime is a distinct block of marks and is the part most often omitted altogether.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the alcohol limit under STCW, and to whom does it apply?
retrieval_cards.answer: Each Administration must establish a limit of not greater than 0.05% blood alcohol level, or 0.25 mg/l alcohol in the breath, or a quantity of alcohol leading to such a concentration, for masters, officers and other seafarers while performing designated safety, security and marine environmental duties.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Not greater than' matters - it is a ceiling on the Administration, not an entitlement for the seafarer, and stricter company limits are lawful.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What records and schedules must be kept, and in what form?
retrieval_cards.answer: Watch schedules must be posted where easily accessible, in a standardized format, in the working language or languages of the ship and in English. Records of the daily hours of rest of seafarers must be maintained in the same standardized format and languages so that compliance can be monitored and verified, and each seafarer must receive a copy of the records pertaining to them, endorsed by the master or a person authorized by the master and by the seafarer.
retrieval_cards.why: This is what a port State control officer actually asks for, and the English-language and countersignature requirements are both marked.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The master suspends the rest schedule during an emergency. Is that the end of the matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The rest requirements need not be maintained in an emergency or in other overriding operational conditions, and the master may require any hours of work necessary for the immediate safety of the ship, persons on board or cargo, or to assist others in distress. But as soon as practicable after the normal situation has been restored, the master must ensure that any seafarers who performed work during a scheduled rest period are provided with an adequate period of rest.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates give the override and stop. The compensating-rest obligation is what makes it a controlled exception rather than a loophole.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your second engineer is on call for an unattended machinery space and is called out twice in the night. What does the Code require?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section A-VIII/1 paragraph 6 states that a seafarer on call, such as when a machinery space is unattended, must have an adequate compensatory rest period if the normal period of rest is disturbed by call-outs to work.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the engineer's own provision and the Code gives UMS as its example, so it is a standard oral follow-up for a Class I candidate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do these criteria actually make a watch safe, rather than merely lawful?
retrieval_cards.answer: Fatigue degrades vigilance, reaction time and judgement without the sufferer detecting it, so self-assessment fails. The criteria replace it with a floor on rest, a shape that guarantees consolidated sleep, removal of a compounding chemical impairment, schedules that force manning to be planned in advance, and records that let flag State, port State and the company's ISM system audit compliance - and regulation VIII/1.1.2 makes the test of the whole system whether the relieving watch is genuinely rested and fit for duty.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the second half of the printed question and carries real marks. Anyone can list the hours; the discussion is what separates a pass from a good answer.

blocks.h: 1. a) What the Goal-Based Standards are, and the gap they close

blocks.p: Traditional SOLAS construction requirements are prescriptive: they say what to fit and how thick to make it. Prescription has two structural weaknesses. It does not say what level of safety is being bought, so nobody can tell whether a rule is generous or marginal; and it freezes technology, because a novel design that is demonstrably as safe may still fail the letter of the rule. Detailed scantling requirements had also migrated almost entirely to classification society rules, over which IMO had no direct oversight - the Organization mandated the outcome but did not govern the rules that actually determined it.

Goal-based standards (GBS) invert this. IMO states the goal and the functional requirements that must be met, and then verifies that the detailed rules - principally class rules - deliver them. GBS was made mandatory by SOLAS regulation II-1/3-10, in force 1 January 2012, with the standards themselves in resolution MSC.287(87) and the verification guidelines in MSC.296(87).

rows: Goals - the high-level objectives to be achieved
Functional requirements - what must be satisfied to meet the goals
Verification of conformity - the procedure for checking Tier IV rules against Tiers I and II
Rules and regulations for ship design and construction - class rules and national requirements
Industry practices and standards - codes, guidelines and safety-management practice

blocks.p: Tiers I to III are the GBS instrument. Tiers IV and V are where the numbers live. The whole design of the system is in that split.

blocks.h: 3. a) The goal, and the functional requirements

blocks.p: The Tier I goal is that ships shall be designed and constructed for a specified design life to be safe and environmentally friendly when properly operated and maintained, under the specified operating and environmental conditions, in intact and specified damage conditions, throughout their life - with a specified design life of not less than 25 years. Note that environmental protection is inside the goal itself, not bolted on.
Tier II converts that into functional requirements, which fall into three natural groups:

ul: Design - design life; the environmental conditions to be designed for (North Atlantic); structural strength; fatigue life; residual strength in a damaged condition; and protection against corrosion, including coating life.
Construction - structural redundancy; watertight and weathertight integrity; human element considerations; design transparency; and construction quality procedures.
In service - survey; maintenance; structural accessibility for inspection; and recycling considerations.

blocks.h: 4. a) Application, and the Ship Construction File

blocks.p: GBS applies to oil tankers and bulk carriers of 150 m in length and above contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2016. The most visible shipboard consequence is the Ship Construction File, required by SOLAS II-1/3-10 and delivering the design transparency functional requirement: the information needed to operate, maintain, repair and respond to an emergency - structural drawings, scantlings, design assumptions, coating specifications and inspection access - kept on board and ashore and maintained through the ship's life.

blocks.h: 5. b) How the framework delivers safety and environmental protection

blocks.p: It works on the hull as the primary barrier. Bulk carriers and tankers were chosen because their failure modes - progressive structural failure, and loss of oil cargo - kill crews and pollute coastlines. Design life, fatigue life, corrosion protection and residual strength after damage attack exactly those modes: a hull that retains strength when damaged is a hull that gives time to evacuate and does not break up. Environmental protection follows from structural integrity, because the overwhelming majority of pollution from these ship types comes from hull failure rather than from operational discharge. Recycling considerations extend the goal to end of life, and structural accessibility ensures the ship can actually be inspected, which is what keeps the design margin real in year twenty rather than only on delivery.

blocks.h: 6. b) Verification - IMO audits the rules, not the ship

blocks.p: This is the structural innovation, and it is what the question is really testing. Under Tier III, an Administration or recognized organization submits its ship construction rules to IMO. An audit team appointed by the Secretary-General assesses whether those rules conform to the Tier I goal and Tier II functional requirements, reports to the Maritime Safety Committee, and the Committee determines conformity. The IACS Common Structural Rules for Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers were the principal submission in the initial round and were confirmed as conforming.

Verification does not stop at the first audit. Maintenance of verification requires rule amendments to be notified and reassessed, with periodic re-verification, so that a rule set cannot drift away from the goals after it has been approved once.

Verification answers are the rules right? Validation answers was this ship actually built to them?, and that runs through the ordinary machinery: plan approval against verified rules, survey during construction, class certification, and statutory certification by or on behalf of the flag State, with the Ship Construction File as the documentary evidence and port State control as the independent check in service. The two together form a closed chain - IMO assures the rules, class and flag assure the ship - and a break at either end defeats the system.

Three things worth saying at management level. First, it brought class rules inside IMO's oversight for the first time, without IMO having to write scantlings. Second, it makes the safety level explicit and auditable rather than implicit in tradition, which is the precondition for the Safety Level Approach now being developed and for applying goal-based methodology to other ship types and to novel technology. Third, for a Chief Engineer the practical residue is the Ship Construction File: it is the ship's design intent in writing, it must be kept current when structural repairs are made, and it is what allows a repair to be judged against the original assumptions rather than against opinion.

Two limbs of eight marks each, and they test different things. Limb (a) is descriptive and countable: the five tiers, the goal, the functional requirements, the application, the Ship Construction File. Put the tiers in a table - it banks five marks in the space of four lines and it is the single most recognisable feature of GBS. Limb (b) is analytical, and it contains an explicit sub-demand - 'the role of verification and validation' - which is where most of the (b) marks sit.

The commonest way to lose limb (b) is to describe verification and validation as vague synonyms for 'checking'. They are not. Give them two separate steps, as steps 6 and 7 do, and say plainly what each one is looking at.

blocks.h: The one distinction that unlocks limb (b)

blocks.p: Verification looks at the RULES. Validation looks at the SHIP.

ul: Verification is a Tier III activity at IMO. A class society submits its construction rules; an audit team assesses them against the Tier I goal and Tier II functional requirements; the MSC determines conformity; and maintenance of verification keeps the assessment alive as the rules are amended. Nobody looks at a ship.

Validation is the ordinary chain that confirms a particular ship was built to those verified rules - plan approval, survey during construction, class and statutory certification, the Ship Construction File, and port State control in service.

blocks.p: If you can state that one sentence and then develop each half, limb (b) is secure.

blocks.h: Why bulk carriers and oil tankers, and not everything

blocks.p: Because that is where the deaths and the spills were. Bulk carrier losses in the late 1980s and 1990s, and tanker structural failures, both had the same root: progressive structural degradation in a hull whose design margin nobody could audit. GBS was written for those two ship types deliberately, as the proving ground for a methodology that IMO intended to generalise later. Saying so shows you understand GBS as a method rather than as a rule about ships over 150 metres.

ul: Giving four tiers, or getting the order wrong. It is five: goals, functional requirements, verification of conformity, rules and regulations, industry practices - and I to III are IMO's.
Saying IMO verifies the ship. It verifies the rules. That is the whole point of the framework.
Treating verification and validation as the same word twice.
Omitting the Ship Construction File. It is the one part of GBS a serving engineer actually handles, and it is the examiner's favourite bridge from theory to the ship.
Claiming GBS applies to all new ships. It is oil tankers and bulk carriers of 150 m and above contracted on or after 1 July 2016.
Answering limb (b) on safety only and never mentioning environmental protection, when the stem names both - and when 'environmentally friendly' is inside the Tier I goal.
Forgetting maintenance of verification. A one-off audit that could never be revisited would be worthless.

'Goal-based' does not mean 'less safe' or 'self-regulated'. It means the required outcome is stated explicitly and the detailed rules are audited against it. If anything it is more demanding than prescription, because the rule-maker must now justify the rule.
The design life of not less than 25 years is a favourite number. So is the North Atlantic environmental condition.
Who does the audit? An audit team appointed by the Secretary-General, reporting to the MSC - not the class society itself, and not the flag State.
Where does the Ship Construction File live? On board and ashore, and it must be kept updated, including after structural repair or modification.
Being asked which tier a class rule sits in. Tier IV.

Being asked how GBS relates to the Safety Level Approach. SLA is the intended development - moving from qualitative goals to a quantified safety level - and at this sitting it is under development, not in force.

quick_revision.recall_15s: What. IMO states the goal and audits the rules against it, instead of prescribing scantlings. Mandatory via SOLAS II-1/3-10 (in force 1 January 2012); standards in MSC.287(87), verification guidelines in MSC.296(87). Five tiers. I goals - II functional requirements - III verification of conformity - IV rules and regulations (class) - V industry practices. I to III are IMO's. Goal. Designed and constructed for a specified design life - not less than 25 years - to be safe and environmentally friendly, in intact and specified damage conditions. Functional requirements. Design (life, North Atlantic, strength, fatigue, residual strength, corrosion), construction (redundancy, watertight integrity, human element, design transparency, quality), in service (survey, maintenance, accessibility, recycling). Applies to. Oil tankers and bulk carriers 150 m and above contracted on or after 1 July 2016. Ship Construction File - design transparency, on board and ashore, kept updated. Verification vs validation. Verification = IMO audit team assesses the RULES against Tiers I and II, MSC determines conformity, and maintenance of verification keeps it alive. Validation = the SHIP - plan approval, survey during construction, class and flag certification, SCF, port State control.

The standards themselves are MSC.287(87) and the verification procedure is MSC.296(87). Naming the SOLAS regulation is what shows the examiner that GBS is treaty law and not a guideline.
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying that IMO verifies the ship. IMO verifies the RULES - a class society submits its construction rules, an audit team appointed by the Secretary-General assesses them against Tiers I and II, and the MSC determines conformity. The individual ship is validated through the ordinary chain of plan approval, survey, class and flag certification. Collapsing verification and validation into one idea loses the core of limb (b).

questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) runs WHY (1), TIERS (2), GOAL (3), PAPER (4). Limb (b) runs PROTECT (5), RULES (6), SHIP (7), SO WHAT (8). The tiers count downwards from IMO to industry - the further down, the more detailed and the less IMO's.
questions.understand_first: The old way of regulating ship construction was to write down the answer: this thickness, that spacing. Two problems followed. Nobody could say how safe a ship built to those numbers actually was - the safety level was buried in tradition rather than stated - and a genuinely better design could be rejected simply for not matching the words. Worse, the numbers themselves had long since moved into classification society rules, which IMO did not govern. Goal-based standards fix all three at once by changing what IMO writes. IMO now writes the goal - a ship that stays safe and environmentally friendly for at least twenty-five years, damaged as well as intact - and the functional requirements underneath it, and then audits the class rules to confirm they deliver it. That is the whole idea, and every detail in this question hangs off it: IMO owns the top three tiers, class owns the numbers, and the check runs upward from the numbers to the goal.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the five tiers of the GBS framework and say who owns each.
retrieval_cards.answer: Tier I goals, Tier II functional requirements and Tier III verification of conformity - all IMO's. Tier IV rules and regulations for ship design and construction, owned by recognized organizations and Administrations. Tier V industry practices and standards. Tiers I to III are the GBS instrument; Tiers IV and V are where the detailed numbers live.
retrieval_cards.why: The five tiers are the most recognisable feature of GBS and the ownership split is the idea behind the whole framework.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the Tier I goal.
retrieval_cards.answer: That ships shall be designed and constructed for a specified design life to be safe and environmentally friendly when properly operated and maintained, under the specified operating and environmental conditions, in intact and specified damage conditions, throughout their life - with a specified design life of not less than 25 years.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Safe and environmentally friendly' is where environmental protection enters GBS, which is exactly what limb (b) of the printed question asks about.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between verification and validation under GBS?
retrieval_cards.answer: Verification looks at the rules: a class society or Administration submits its ship construction rules to IMO, an audit team appointed by the Secretary-General assesses them against the Tier I goal and Tier II functional requirements, the MSC determines conformity, and maintenance of verification keeps that assessment current as rules are amended. Validation looks at the ship: plan approval, survey during construction, class and statutory certification, the Ship Construction File and port State control confirm that this particular ship was built to those verified rules.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the core of limb (b) and the distinction most candidates fail to make.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Ship Construction File and where must it be kept?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is the file required by SOLAS II-1/3-10 that delivers the design-transparency functional requirement. It contains the information needed to operate, maintain, repair and respond to an emergency - structural drawings, scantlings, design assumptions, coating specifications and inspection access - and it must be kept both on board and ashore and maintained throughout the ship's life.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the one element of GBS a serving engineer handles, and the usual bridge from theory to the ship in an oral.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which ships does GBS apply to, and from when?
retrieval_cards.answer: Oil tankers of 150 m in length and above and bulk carriers of 150 m in length and above, contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2016. The framework became mandatory through SOLAS regulation II-1/3-10, in force 1 January 2012.
retrieval_cards.why: Two different dates - when the regulation came into force and when the standards bite on a contract - and candidates routinely merge them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does IMO approve your ship's scantlings under GBS?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. IMO verifies the RULES, not the ship. The class society's construction rules are submitted and audited against the Tier I goal and Tier II functional requirements; the scantlings for a particular ship remain a Tier IV matter for those verified class rules, and compliance of the ship is confirmed by plan approval, survey and certification.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most common misconception about GBS, and a favourite oral question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A class society amends its verified construction rules. What must happen?
retrieval_cards.answer: Maintenance of verification applies. Rule amendments must be notified to IMO and reassessed against the Tier I goal and Tier II functional requirements, with periodic re-verification, so that a rule set cannot drift away from the goals after being approved once.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates give the initial audit and stop. Without maintenance of verification the framework would decay the first time a rule changed.

blocks.h: 1. What the 2023 Strategy is, and what it replaced

blocks.p: The 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships was adopted by resolution MEPC.377(80) on 7 July 2023, and it expressly revokes the 2018 Initial Strategy from that date. It is a policy instrument, not law: it binds nobody directly, and it works by committing the Committee to develop measures which then become law as amendments to MARPOL Annex VI. The Committee also agreed to keep it under review with a view to adopting a further revised Strategy in 2028.

blocks.h: 2. The vision and the levels of ambition

blocks.p: The vision is to reduce GHG emissions from international shipping and, as a matter of urgency, to phase them out as soon as possible, while promoting a just and equitable transition. Four levels of ambition follow:

ol: Carbon intensity of the ship to decline through further improvement of energy efficiency for new ships, reviewing with the aim of strengthening the design requirements.
Carbon intensity of international shipping to decline - CO2 per transport work to fall, as a fleet average, by at least 40% by 2030 against 2008.
Uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and/or energy sources to reach at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used by international shipping by 2030.
Net zero - to peak emissions as soon as possible and reach net-zero GHG emissions by or around, i.e. close to, 2050, taking into account different national circumstances.

blocks.p: Two features change everything. The targets are GHG, not CO2 alone, so methane and nitrous oxide count - which bears directly on LNG. And they are measured well-to-wake under the LCA guidelines (MEPC.376(80)), so a fuel that is clean at the funnel but dirty to produce earns no credit.
The levels of ambition are intensity-based; the checkpoints are absolute, and they are what make the pathway real - to reduce total annual GHG emissions from international shipping, against 2008, by:

ul: at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030; and
at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040.

blocks.p: They are indicative - checkpoints on the way to net zero, not binding limits - and the 'striving for' figures are the compromise that allowed adoption.

These constrain how any measure may be designed, and they are why the mid-term measures took so long. They include non-discrimination and no more favourable treatment as enshrined in MARPOL; common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities in the light of different national circumstances, from the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement; that all ships give full and complete effect regardless of flag; the need to consider impacts on States, in particular LDCs and SIDS; and evidence-based decision-making balanced with the precautionary approach. The first two pull in opposite directions - one says treat every ship alike, the other says treat States differently - and the whole negotiation on a GHG price is an attempt to reconcile them.

blocks.h: 5. The short-term measures - already in force

blocks.p: The short-term measures are those finalized between 2018 and 2023, and they are operative today under MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4: the EEDI for new ships, the EEXI for existing ships, the SEEMP, the fuel oil consumption data collection system, and the operational carbon intensity rating (CII). The Strategy requires their review, and requires the mid-term measures to be designed in synergy with them - CII is named expressly.
This is the core of the question. The Strategy requires a basket comprising both elements together, to be finalized and agreed by 2025:

ol: a technical element - a goal-based marine fuel standard regulating the phased reduction of the GHG intensity of marine fuel, on a well-to-wake basis; and
an economic element - a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism.

blocks.p: The logic of pairing them is that the standard compels the transition while the price funds and accelerates it and closes the cost gap between fossil and zero-carbon fuel. Both are subject to a comprehensive impact assessment of effects on States. Other candidate mid-term measures - annual emission estimates, R&D, port and operational efficiency, national action plans - sit alongside the basket.

The Strategy deliberately does not specify long-term measures. They are defined only as measures finalized and agreed beyond 2030, to be developed as part of the 2028 review, once the mid-term basket is in force and its effect can be measured. That is an honest position rather than a gap: the 2040 checkpoint and net zero cannot be delivered by a fuel standard alone, but what is added should depend on evidence that does not yet exist.

blocks.h: 8. Where the process stood at this examination

blocks.p: The Strategy's own milestone table places this sitting exactly. MEPC 81 (spring 2024) has happened - the interim impact-assessment report and the finalization of the basket. MEPC 82 (autumn 2024) has not; the finalized impact assessment is due there. Approval of the measures is scheduled for MEPC 83 in spring 2025, adoption at an extraordinary MEPC session about six months later, and entry into force 16 months after adoption, in 2027. So at this date: the architecture is agreed and nothing is adopted. Any answer that describes a binding IMO carbon price or fuel-intensity limit as existing law is wrong for September 2024.

blocks.h: 9. The potential impact on the shipping industry

blocks.p: Six consequences follow, and they are where the evaluation marks are. Fuel cost becomes the dominant variable: a GHG price plus a tightening intensity standard converts an environmental obligation into an operating-cost line, and the well-to-wake basis decides which fuels actually qualify. Newbuilding choice becomes a risk decision - a ship ordered today trades into the 2040 checkpoint, so dual-fuel and retrofit-ready design is bought as optionality against asset stranding. The methane question is sharpened, because a GHG target measured well-to-wake treats slip as emissions. Commercial terms must change: the party that buys the fuel and the party that directs the speed are usually different, so the cost must be allocated in the charterparty. Crew competence and safety become the limiting factor - the resolution itself acknowledges the human element in safe implementation, and ammonia and hydrogen raise toxicity and containment problems that training and the safety framework must reach before the fuels do. And regulatory fragmentation is the risk a global measure exists to cure: with the EU Emissions Trading System already extended to shipping from 1 January 2024, a ship on a European trade already pays for carbon under a regional scheme, which is precisely the outcome the guiding principle of no more favourable treatment is meant to prevent.

The stem sets three tasks and the marks are lost by answering only the first. Discuss the key elements (steps 1-5), explain the midterm and long-term measures (steps 6-7), and evaluate their potential impact on the shipping industry (step 9). The word evaluate is the highest command verb on the paper and it is worth real marks; an answer that recites targets and stops has answered a third of the question.

Step 8 is not in the printed stem, but it is what makes the answer correct for this sitting. Stating where the process actually stood in September 2024 - basket agreed, nothing adopted - is both the honest position and a strong discriminator.

blocks.h: Get the two families of numbers apart

blocks.p: This is the single most common failure on this question, and it is entirely avoidable.

ul: Levels of ambition are mostly about intensity - CO2 per transport work down at least 40% by 2030, and zero or near-zero fuels at at least 5%, striving for 10%, by 2030. Plus net zero by or around 2050.
Indicative checkpoints are about total annual GHG emissions - at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030, and at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040.

blocks.p: So 40% is intensity and 20% is absolute, both by 2030 and both against 2008. Candidates constantly quote the 20% as an intensity target or the 40% as an absolute one. Write the two lists under separate headings and the confusion cannot happen.

ul: GHG, not CO2. The 2018 Strategy spoke of CO2; the 2023 Strategy speaks of greenhouse gases. Methane and nitrous oxide are in scope, which is why methane slip from LNG became a live commercial issue.

Well-to-wake, not tank-to-wake. Section 3.2 requires the ambitions and checkpoints to take account of well-to-wake emissions under the LCA guidelines, expressly so that emissions are not simply shifted to another sector. A 'zero-emission' fuel made with fossil energy is not zero.
Quoting the 2018 Initial Strategy targets - 40% intensity by 2030 and 50% absolute by 2050. The 2023 Strategy revoked it.
Saying 'net zero by 2050' flatly. The text is 'by or around, i.e. close to, 2050', and that hedge was the price of consensus.
Dropping the 'striving for' figures, which are half of each checkpoint.
Forgetting the zero or near-zero fuel uptake ambition - 5% striving for 10% by 2030. It is the only ambition expressed as a share of energy used.
Describing the mid-term measures as a single measure. It is a basket of two, technical and economic, and the Strategy requires both.
Calling the technical element a fuel type mandate. It is a goal-based fuel standard on GHG intensity - it does not name a fuel.
Inventing long-term measures. The Strategy defines them only by timing - beyond 2030, developed in the 2028 review.
Answering the whole question without ever saying what any of it does to a shipowner.

blocks.h: The date of this paper - the sharpest temporal edge on the whole paper

blocks.p: MEPC 82 opened on 30 September 2024, at or after the end of this examination month. The most recent MEPC at this sitting is MEPC 81, in March 2024. Three consequences follow and each one is a way to get the answer wrong.

ul: The IMO Net-Zero Framework and the GHG Fuel Intensity measure did not exist. That name and that mechanism came out of MEPC 83 in April 2025. Writing them into a September 2024 answer is an anachronism, and it is the single most likely error on this question because almost all study material now written on this topic uses them.
MEPC.395(82), the 2024 SEEMP Guidelines adopted on 4 October 2024, did not exist. The operative SEEMP development guidelines at this sitting are MEPC.346(78) of 2022.

FuelEU Maritime was adopted but applies only from 1 January 2025, so it must not be described as applying. The EU ETS, by contrast, had been extended to maritime transport from 1 January 2024 and was operative - that one is safe to cite, and is the better example of regional fragmentation.

blocks.p: The correct sitting position is stated in one sentence: the architecture of the mid-term measures is agreed and nothing is adopted.

ul: Against what baseline? 2008, for every reduction figure in the Strategy.
Is the Strategy law? No. It is a policy instrument; the law is MARPOL Annex VI, and the measures become law as amendments to it.
Are the checkpoints binding? They are indicative. The levels of ambition are the commitment; the checkpoints mark the path.
Why both a standard and a price? The standard compels; the price funds the transition and closes the cost gap. The Strategy requires the basket to contain both.
What does 'just and equitable transition' mean here? It is in the vision, and it is operationalised through the impact assessment on States, particularly LDCs and SIDS.
How does this interact with CII? Section 4.8 expressly requires synergies with existing measures such as the CII to be considered.
What replaced the Initial Strategy, and when?
State the 2030 and 2040 checkpoints, with the striving figures.
Is that 40% absolute or intensity?
What are the two elements of the mid-term basket?
What does well-to-wake mean, and why does it matter for LNG?
Your owner asks whether to order a dual-fuel ship. What do you tell him?
How would a GHG price be shared between owner and charterer?
What new hazards come with ammonia as a fuel, and is the crew trained for them?

blocks.p: Nine steps in three blocks. WHAT IT IS - the Strategy and what it revoked (1), the vision and ambitions (2), the checkpoints (3), the principles (4). WHAT IT DOES - short-term already in force (5), the mid-term basket (6), long-term deferred to 2028 (7). WHERE WE ARE AND WHAT IT COSTS - the sitting position (8) and the industry impact (9).

For the numbers, hold one pair and one hedge: 40 intensity / 20 absolute by 2030, and net zero by or around 2050. Then the second checkpoint is 70 by 2040, and the fuel-uptake ambition is 5 striving 10. Every 'at least' has a 'striving for' behind it.

questions.understand_first: The Strategy is not a rule and it does not make anybody do anything. It is the Organization writing down, in one place, how much the shipping industry must reduce, by when, and by what process the binding rules will be produced - and that third part is the one candidates skip. Read it as three layers stacked on each other. At the top is a destination: net zero by or around 2050. Underneath are waypoints - the levels of ambition, which are mostly about intensity, and the indicative checkpoints, which are about total emissions and are the ones that actually test whether the world fleet is on track. At the bottom is a schedule for making law: short-term measures already in MARPOL Annex VI, a mid-term basket to be agreed by 2025, and long-term measures deliberately left blank until 2028. Everything else in the question - why the basket has two halves, why the principles matter, why the industry is investing in dual-fuel ships - falls out of that structure. retrieval_cards.prompt: State the four levels of ambition.
retrieval_cards.answer: One, carbon intensity of the ship to decline through further improvement of energy efficiency for new ships. Two, carbon intensity of international shipping to decline - CO2 per transport work down by at least 40% by 2030 compared to 2008. Three, uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and energy sources to be at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used by international shipping by 2030. Four, to peak GHG emissions as soon as possible and reach net zero by or around, i.e. close to, 2050.
retrieval_cards.why: Four ambitions, and the fuel-uptake one is the most commonly forgotten. 'By or around' is the exact wording.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the indicative checkpoints and say how they differ from the levels of ambition.
retrieval_cards.answer: To reduce total annual GHG emissions from international shipping by at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030, and by at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040, both compared to 2008. They differ because they are measured on TOTAL ANNUAL EMISSIONS, whereas the corresponding level of ambition is measured on carbon intensity - CO2 per transport work. They are also indicative rather than binding.
retrieval_cards.why: 40% intensity against 20% absolute, both by 2030 against 2008, is the single most confused pair of numbers on this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the two elements of the basket of mid-term measures, and why both?
retrieval_cards.answer: A technical element - a goal-based marine fuel standard regulating the phased reduction of the marine fuel's GHG intensity - and an economic element, on the basis of a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism. Both are required together. The standard compels the transition by tightening what may be burned; the price funds and accelerates it and narrows the cost gap between fossil and zero or near-zero fuels.
retrieval_cards.why: Describing the mid-term measures as one measure loses the core of the question. The Strategy requires the basket to comprise both.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does well-to-wake mean here, and why did the Strategy adopt it?
retrieval_cards.answer: That the GHG emissions of a marine fuel are counted across its whole life cycle - production, processing and transport as well as combustion on board - under the LCA guidelines in resolution MEPC.376(80). The Strategy adopted it so that emissions are reduced within the energy system of international shipping and are not simply shifted to another sector by a fuel that is clean at the funnel but carbon-intensive to make.
retrieval_cards.why: It decides which fuels actually count as zero or near-zero, and it is why methane slip became a commercial problem for LNG.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where had the mid-term measures actually got to by September 2024?
retrieval_cards.answer: The architecture was agreed and nothing was adopted. MEPC 81 in spring 2024 had produced the interim impact-assessment report and finalized the basket; MEPC 82 had not yet opened. Approval was scheduled for MEPC 83 in spring 2025, adoption at an extraordinary session about six months later, and entry into force 16 months after adoption, in 2027.
retrieval_cards.why: The IMO Net-Zero Framework and the GHG Fuel Intensity measure did not exist at this sitting. Writing them in is the commonest way to get this question wrong today.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the 2023 Strategy legally binding, and what did it do to the 2018 Strategy?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is not binding. It is a policy instrument adopted by resolution MEPC.377(80) on 7 July 2023; the binding law is MARPOL Annex VI, and the Strategy's measures take legal effect only when adopted as amendments to it. Its operative paragraph 6 provides that the 2023 Strategy revokes the 2018 Initial IMO GHG Strategy as from that date.
retrieval_cards.why: Quoting the Initial Strategy's targets is a straight error, and knowing the Strategy is policy rather than law is what lets you explain why the timetable to 2027 exists at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your owner asks whether to order a conventional or a dual-fuel ship. What does the Strategy imply?
retrieval_cards.answer: A ship ordered now will still be trading at the 2040 checkpoint, when total annual emissions must be at least 70% below 2008. A conventional single-fuel ship therefore carries asset-stranding risk, and dual-fuel or retrofit-ready design is bought as optionality rather than as an immediate saving. The answer also depends on well-to-wake accounting - which decides whether the alternative fuel actually counts - on the future cost gap once a GHG price applies, and on whether crews can be trained and the ship operated safely on that fuel.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the evaluation mark. It turns the targets into the commercial decision the examiner wants a management-level candidate to be able to reason about.

blocks.h: 1. Where the Funds sit - a three-tier system

blocks.p: The IOPC Funds are not a stand-alone regime. They are the second and third tiers of a layered compensation system for pollution by persistent oil carried as cargo in bulk by a tanker:

rows: CLC 92 - strict liability, channelled exclusively to the registered owner, with its own tonnage-based limits and compulsory insurance with direct action
2003 Supplementary Fund Protocol - the Supplementary Fund, optional for States
Oil receivers in States that have joined it

blocks.p: The design principle is shared burden: the shipowner carries the first layer, and the cargo interest - the industry whose oil is being moved - carries the layers above it. The older 1971 Fund has been wound up and no longer exists.

blocks.h: 2. The role and functions of the Funds

blocks.p: The primary role is to pay compensation where CLC alone does not produce it, in three situations: where the shipowner is exempt from liability under CLC; where the shipowner is financially incapable of meeting the claim and his insurance is insufficient; and - the usual case - where the damage exceeds the CLC limit.

Around that sit the working functions: assessing and settling claims, usually through a joint claims office with the shipowner's P&I club so that a claimant deals with one process; publishing the Claims Manual that tells claimants what is admissible before they claim; attending casualties and monitoring clean-up so that costs are controlled while they are being incurred; taking part in legal proceedings; and contributing the accumulated claims experience back into IMO's work.
This is the feature that most distinguishes the Funds, and it is the most commonly misunderstood. The Funds are not financed by governments, and not by shipowners.

ul: Contributions are levied on any person who received, in a calendar year, more than 150,000 tonnes of contributing oil - crude oil and heavy fuel oil - carried by sea and received in a port or terminal installation in a Member State.
The obligation falls on the receiver, and the threshold is applied to the receiver, not to the State - so a State with many small receivers may contribute very little.
States report annual oil receipts; the Assembly then levies annual contributions according to what the Fund actually needs, so it is a post-event, pay-as-you-go system rather than a standing reserve.
For the Supplementary Fund a minimum aggregate quantity is deemed to have been received in each Member State, so that a State with little oil import still bears a floor share.

blocks.p: Two industry agreements, STOPIA 2006 and TOPIA 2006, sit voluntarily on top of this: tanker owners' P&I interests indemnify the 1992 Fund in respect of small tankers, and indemnify the Supplementary Fund for a share of its payments, rebalancing the burden between shipowners and oil receivers without amending the Conventions.

blocks.h: 4. Eligibility - which incidents and which damage

blocks.p: The gateway conditions are narrow and are where most refused claims fail:

ul: the oil must be persistent oil carried as cargo in bulk by a tanker - non-persistent oil such as gas oil is outside, and so are bunkers spilled from a non-tanker, which belong to the Bunker Convention;
the damage must occur in the territory, territorial sea or exclusive economic zone of a Member State, with preventive measures compensable wherever taken;

the categories of admissible damage are property damage, clean-up and preventive measures, consequential economic loss to those whose property was contaminated, pure economic loss where the link of causation is close enough - the fisherman or hotelier whose property was never touched - and reasonable measures of reinstatement of the environment;
claims are time-barred on the same terms as CLC: three years from the date of the damage and six years from the incident.

blocks.p: The Claims Manual reduces admissibility to four tests, and a claim must pass all of them. The expense or loss must have been actually incurred, not projected. The measures must be reasonable and justifiable when judged objectively at the time. The loss must be quantifiable and supported by documentary evidence. And there must be a reasonable degree of proximity - a sufficiently close link of causation between the contamination and the loss.

One restriction does more work than the others: compensation for impairment of the environment, other than loss of profit from that impairment, is limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken. There is no compensation for environmental damage as such, and no abstract theoretical valuation of a damaged ecosystem is admissible.

blocks.h: 6. The limits, and what happens at the ceiling

blocks.p: The total payable by the 1992 Fund for any one incident - including the sum actually paid under CLC - is 203 million SDR, rising to 300,740,000 SDR where three Member States collectively received 600 million tonnes or more of contributing oil. Where the Supplementary Fund applies, the total available including CLC and the 1992 Fund is 750 million SDR.

If admitted claims exceed the ceiling, the Fund does not pay in full and does not pay first-come-first-served: it pays pro rata, so every claimant receives the same percentage. In a large casualty the Fund therefore makes interim payments at a reduced percentage until the total exposure is known - which is prudent, and is also why victims of the biggest spills wait longest.

blocks.h: 7. Effectiveness - what the system does well

blocks.p: Judged against what preceded it, the regime works. Strict liability removes the need to prove fault; compulsory insurance with direct action means there is always a solvent defendant; and the tiers mean the money does not stop at the shipowner's limit. The overwhelming majority of claims are settled without litigation, because the Claims Manual tells claimants in advance what will be paid and the Funds and the P&I club assess jointly. And the burden is shared between ship and cargo, which is the political achievement that made a fund possible at all - the receivers of the oil pay for the risk of moving it.

Four criticisms are fair and should be made. The ceiling can be exhausted: a major spill on a developed coastline can generate admitted claims beyond even the Supplementary Fund, and the consequence is pro-rata payment and years of delay. Pure economic loss and environmental damage are tightly restricted - the proximity test excludes claimants who suffered real loss, and reinstatement-only recovery means the ecological harm itself is never compensated. The third tier is optional, so the protection a coastal community actually has depends on whether its State joined the Supplementary Fund Protocol - the very States most exposed and least able to absorb loss are often those that have not. And the scope is narrow: it reaches only persistent oil from tankers, so a large containership bunker spill, an HNS release or a non-persistent product spill falls to other regimes with lower limits or, in some cases, to none.

The honest verdict is that the regime is very effective at what it was designed to do and is deliberately not designed to do more. It guarantees prompt, predictable compensation for quantifiable loss from tanker oil spills; it does not, and does not attempt to, place a price on environmental harm.

The ship pays first, then the cargo pays. That single sentence is the political and structural core of the whole regime. A tanker's limitation amount will not cover a major spill, and raising it without limit would make tankers uninsurable - so the drafters went to the other beneficiary of the voyage, the oil industry that receives the cargo, and levied the second and third tiers on receivers. Once you have that, the 150,000-tonne threshold, the annual levy, the pay-as-you-go structure and even STOPIA and TOPIA all follow logically.

ul: Saying the Funds are financed by governments or by shipowners. They are financed by receivers of contributing oil. This is the single most common error on this question.
Forgetting that the threshold is more than 150,000 tonnes of contributing oil received in a calendar year, and that contributing oil is crude oil and heavy fuel oil - not every petroleum product.

Giving the admissibility criteria as a vague 'reasonableness' test. There are four - actually incurred, reasonable and justifiable, quantifiable and evidenced, sufficiently proximate.
Answering the effectiveness limb with praise only. The examiner has asked you to evaluate; a one-sided answer reads as an advertisement.
Persistent oil, as cargo, in a tanker. All three conditions must hold. Expect to be given a scenario that fails one of them.

Pro rata, not first come first served. When claims exceed the ceiling, everyone is paid the same percentage - which is why the Funds make interim payments at a reduced level until the exposure is known.
The Supplementary Fund is optional. Whether a coastal State's citizens have a third tier depends on whether that State joined the 2003 Protocol.
SDR, not dollars. The Special Drawing Right is the IMF unit of account, and the limits move with it as well as by amendment.
Three years and six years - the same time bar as CLC, and the right is extinguished rather than merely barred.
STOPIA and TOPIA are voluntary industry agreements, not treaty amendments. Knowing that they exist, and that they push burden back towards shipowners, is a strong mark.

questions.understand_first: Start from the problem the drafters faced. A tanker owner's liability has to be limited, or nobody would insure a tanker; but a major spill costs far more than any limit a shipowner could carry. So the money has to come from somewhere else, and the drafters went to the only other party who profits from the voyage - the oil industry that receives the cargo. That is the whole idea of the IOPC Funds: the ship pays first and the cargo pays next. Everything the question asks about follows from it. The funding mechanism is a levy on receivers of oil, not on States or shipowners. The eligibility rules are narrow because the receivers only agreed to underwrite one specific risk - persistent oil, carried as cargo, in a tanker. The admissibility criteria are strict because a fund financed by levy has to be able to predict and control what it pays. And the ceiling exists because a contributory fund with unlimited exposure is not a fund at all. Judge the regime against that design and it is a considerable success; judge it as a general remedy for marine environmental harm and it looks mean - which is why the effectiveness limb needs both halves.
