blocks.h: 1. a) Where social security sits in the MLC

blocks.p: The MLC is built in five Titles, and Title 4 is 'Health protection, medical care, welfare and social security protection'. It runs in a deliberate sequence: Regulation 4.1 medical care on board and ashore, 4.2 shipowners' liability, 4.3 health and safety protection and accident prevention, 4.4 access to shore-based welfare facilities, and 4.5 social security. The first four are what the shipowner must provide during the engagement; 4.5 is what the STATE must provide, and it reaches beyond the voyage into old age, invalidity and the seafarer's family.

Regulation 4.5 imposes three duties. Each Member must ensure that all seafarers and, to the extent provided in national law, their dependants have access to social security protection. Each Member undertakes to take steps, according to national circumstances and through international cooperation, to achieve progressively comprehensive protection. And seafarers subject to its social security legislation must be entitled to protection no less favourable than that enjoyed by shoreworkers.

Two features are distinctive. The obligation is progressive rather than immediate - the Convention accepts that a State cannot deliver everything at once. And the benchmark is parity with shoreworkers, not an absolute standard: the test is whether the seafarer is treated worse than a shore employee of the same State.

blocks.h: 3. a) Standard A4.5 - the nine branches and the minimum

blocks.p: The mandatory Code names nine branches of social security to be considered:

ol: medical care
sickness benefit
unemployment benefit
old-age benefit
employment injury benefit
family benefit
maternity benefit
invalidity benefit
survivors' benefit

blocks.p: These complement - they do not replace - the protection under Regulations 4.1 and 4.2. At the time of ratification a Member must provide at least three of the nine, and Guideline B4.5 recommends that those three should at least be medical care, sickness benefit and employment injury benefit. Each Member specifies its branches at ratification and notifies the Director-General of any it adds later; the Director-General maintains a register.

blocks.h: 4. a) How the protection is delivered

blocks.p: Standard A4.5 is deliberately flexible about the machinery. Protection may sit in laws or regulations, in private schemes, in collective bargaining agreements, or in a combination. Where coverage in a branch is inadequate, the Member must consider comparable benefits by other means. Members must cooperate, through bilateral or multilateral agreements, to maintain rights acquired or in the course of acquisition regardless of residence - the portability problem that arises when a seafarer works for foreign employers all his life. And each Member must provide fair and effective procedures for the settlement of disputes.

The critical allocation is in paragraph 3: complementary protection is owed by the State to all seafarers ordinarily resident in its territory. Social security therefore follows residence, not the flag - which is the opposite of most of the Convention and is the provision that matters most to a labour-supplying country.

Two later amendment sets reinforce this from the shipowner's side and were in force at this sitting: the 2014 amendments requiring financial security for abandonment and for contractual claims arising from death or long-term disability, and the 2018 amendments continuing wages and entitlements while a seafarer is held captive as a result of piracy or armed robbery.

India is a party to the MLC and a major labour-supplying State, which makes Standard A4.5 paragraph 3 - the ordinary residence obligation - the operative provision for it, because a large proportion of Indian seafarers serve on foreign-flag ships and are therefore outside India's flag State chain altogether. The Convention takes effect in India through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and rules made under it, with the Directorate General of Shipping as competent authority, which inspects and certifies Indian ships and exercises port State control over foreign ships.

ul: Welfare board and welfare fund machinery for seafarers, financing hostels, medical facilities, recreation and shore welfare - the direct counterpart of Regulation 4.4.
The Seamen's Provident Fund, a contributory scheme providing an old-age and retirement benefit for seafarers within its scope.
Licensing and regulation of recruitment and placement services by the Administration, so that seafarers are recruited only through approved agencies and are not charged fees for employment.

The Indian National Database of Seafarers and the seafarer identity document scheme, which give every seafarer a verifiable identity and service record - the precondition for claiming any entitlement years later.
Medical examination standards and an approved-doctor system, supporting the medical-care and fitness limbs.
Online grievance redressal and e-governance channels through the Administration, for complaints about wages, contracts, abandonment and recruitment abuse.
Training capacity and its regulation, which is welfare in the practical sense that employability is what secures the income the other benefits are calculated on.

blocks.h: 7. b) How they align with the MLC - and where they do not

blocks.p: The alignment is real and can be stated precisely. The welfare board machinery answers Regulation 4.4; the provident fund answers the old-age branch; the medical examination and approved-doctor system supports medical care; recruitment regulation answers Regulation 1.4; and the identity and database schemes make the portability duty in Standard A4.5 paragraph 8 administratively possible. Because a Member need only provide three of the nine branches at ratification, and because protection may be delivered through private schemes and collective agreements as well as legislation, a mixed system of this kind is squarely within what the Convention contemplates.

Three gaps are worth stating honestly, and they are what turns a list into an answer. First, unemployment benefit is among the hardest branches to deliver for a workforce engaged voyage by voyage, and the gap between contracts is precisely when a seafarer is most exposed. Second, the foreign-flag problem: the seafarer resident in India but employed on a foreign ship is protected by Regulation 4.5 through residence, yet the practical machinery - the shipowner, the P&I cover, the collective agreement - all sits abroad, so the State's obligation is easier to state than to enforce. Third, portability under paragraph 8 depends on bilateral and multilateral agreements, and rights acquired under a foreign employer are only as secure as the agreements that carry them home.

The fair conclusion is that India's initiatives satisfy the Convention's architecture - a minimum set of branches, delivered by mixed means, benchmarked against shore employment - while the progressive obligation in Regulation 4.5.2 remains genuinely unfinished, which is what that word is there to acknowledge.

Two limbs of eight. Limb (a) is countable and the marks are concentrated in one place: the nine branches and the three-branch minimum. Write the nine as a numbered list - never as prose - because that is how they are marked, and add the three-branch rule and Guideline B4.5's recommended three immediately afterwards. Limb (b) is evaluative: 'how do these initiatives align with the MLC's requirements' is a comparison, so every Indian initiative should be tied to the MLC provision it answers, and the answer must be willing to say where alignment is incomplete.

The single strongest move available in this question is to notice that Standard A4.5 paragraph 3 attaches the obligation to ORDINARY RESIDENCE, not to the flag. That is why limb (b) exists at all: India's duty to its seafarers does not depend on which flag they serve under. Say that once, and limb (b) stops being a list of schemes and becomes an argument.

Almost the whole MLC allocates duties to the shipowner and enforces them through the flag. Social security cannot work that way. A pension, an invalidity benefit or a survivor's benefit is paid decades after the engagement ends, long after the shipowner and the flag have gone; and a seafarer typically works for a series of foreign employers with no continuous national employer at all. So Title 4 changes the connecting factor: the State of ordinary residence takes the responsibility. Once you see that, the three-branch minimum, the progressive obligation, the cooperation duty on portability and the whole Indian limb all follow.

ul: Giving eight branches, or ten. There are nine, and the ones dropped are usually family benefit and maternity benefit.
Saying a Member must provide all nine. It must provide at least three at ratification and work progressively towards comprehensive coverage.

Confusing Guideline B4.5's recommended three - medical care, sickness benefit, employment injury benefit - with a mandatory requirement. The Guideline is not mandatory; the Standard's requirement is any three.

Confusing Regulation 4.5 with Regulation 4.2, shipowners' liability. 4.2 is the shipowner's obligation during and shortly after engagement; 4.5 is the State's, and it reaches into old age and survivorship.
Writing limb (b) as a list of Indian schemes with no reference back to any MLC provision. The stem asks how they align.
Inventing circular numbers, scheme names or benefit amounts to make limb (b) look authoritative. An unsupported number is worse than a stated gap.
Presenting the 2022 amendments as being in force. They entered into force 23 December 2024, after this sitting.
Citing the Merchant Shipping Act 2025. It commenced 15 March 2026. For this sitting the framework is the Merchant Shipping Act 1958.
'No less favourable than shoreworkers.' The benchmark is comparative, not absolute - which is why a State with modest shore provision is not in breach for having modest seafarer provision.
'Progressively comprehensive.' The Convention builds in gradualism deliberately. Quoting that phrase shows you have read the Regulation rather than a summary.
Ordinary residence, not flag. The most examinable feature of the whole provision.
Where may the protection live? In laws, in private schemes, in collective bargaining agreements, or a combination. Candidates assume legislation only.
The register. Members specify their branches at ratification and notify the Director-General of additions, who keeps a register - a small point that is very rarely given.

Portability. Standard A4.5 paragraph 8 requires cooperation to maintain rights acquired or in the course of acquisition regardless of residence. It is the provision that matters most to a career spent under foreign employers.
The 2014 abandonment financial security amendments are a favourite bridge from social security to a real casualty. They were in force at this sitting.

blocks.h: The sitting date - what was and was not in force

blocks.p: Two dates decide whether this answer is right for September 2024.

ul: The MLC 2022 amendments were NOT in force. They were approved by the International Labour Conference at its 110th Session in 2022 - before this sitting - but entered into force on 23 December 2024, three months after it. Approved is not in force. The operative text at this sitting is the Convention as amended through the 2018 set, which entered into force 26 December 2020.
The Merchant Shipping Act 2025 did not exist. It commenced 15 March 2026. Every Indian statutory reference in this answer is to the framework of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958.

blocks.p: One point of method is worth recording, because it is how this answer avoided a subtle error. The consolidated MLC text held in the corpus is a post-sitting edition that includes the 2022 amendments. Rather than assume that Standard A4.5 was unaffected, its text was extracted from three separate ILO editions and compared mechanically. It is character-identical in all three, so it is safe to quote for September 2024. Quoting a post-sitting consolidation without that check is exactly how a temporal error gets into an otherwise correct answer.

blocks.p: Limb (a) is WHERE (1) - WHAT THE STATE OWES (2) - THE NINE (3) - HOW IT IS DELIVERED (4). Limb (b) is INDIA'S POSITION (5) - THE INITIATIVES (6) - ALIGNMENT AND GAPS (7).

For the nine branches, run them in the order of a working life and none is lost: you get ill (medical care, sickness benefit), you get hurt at work (employment injury), you are out of work (unemployment), you have a family (family benefit, maternity), you are permanently disabled (invalidity), you retire (old-age), you die (survivors'). Nine, in life order. Then three at ratification, and the Guideline's three are medical care, sickness, injury.

questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) runs WHERE (1), WHAT THE STATE OWES (2), THE NINE (3), HOW DELIVERED (4). Limb (b) runs POSITION (5), INITIATIVES (6), ALIGNMENT AND GAPS (7). Recall the nine branches in the order of a working life: ill, hurt at work, out of work, family, disabled, retired, dead.
questions.understand_first: Nearly all of the MLC works the same way: it puts a duty on the shipowner and enforces it through the flag State, with the maritime labour certificate as the proof. Social security cannot work like that, and understanding why is the whole question. A pension, an invalidity benefit or a widow's benefit falls due decades after the engagement ends, when the shipowner may no longer exist and the ship has changed flag three times; and a typical seafarer's career is a series of short contracts with foreign employers, so there is no continuous national employer to attach the obligation to. Title 4 therefore switches the connecting factor from the flag to the State where the seafarer ordinarily lives. That single move explains everything else in the question: why the duty is on the Member rather than the shipowner, why it is expressed as progressive rather than immediate, why only three of nine branches are required at ratification, why the Convention insists on cooperation to keep rights portable - and why an Indian limb belongs in the question at all, since India owes duties to its resident seafarers no matter whose flag they sail under.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the nine branches of social security under Standard A4.5.
retrieval_cards.answer: Medical care, sickness benefit, unemployment benefit, old-age benefit, employment injury benefit, family benefit, maternity benefit, invalidity benefit and survivors' benefit.
retrieval_cards.why: Nine exactly. Family benefit and maternity benefit are the two most often dropped, and the list is the largest single block of marks in limb (a).

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many branches must a Member provide, and which does the Guideline recommend?
retrieval_cards.answer: At the time of ratification the protection must include at least three of the nine branches. Guideline B4.5 recommends that those should at least include medical care, sickness benefit and employment injury benefit - but the Guideline is non-mandatory, so any three satisfy the Standard. The Member specifies its branches at ratification and notifies the Director-General of any added later, who maintains a register.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying all nine are required is a straight error, and the mandatory-versus-recommended distinction is a favourite discriminator.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does MLC social security follow the flag or the seafarer?
retrieval_cards.answer: The seafarer. Standard A4.5 paragraph 3 requires each Member to take steps to provide complementary social security protection to all seafarers ORDINARILY RESIDENT in its territory, no less favourable than that enjoyed by shoreworkers resident there. Flag State responsibility under paragraph 5 is confined to Regulations 4.1 and 4.2 - medical care and shipowners' liability.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the most examinable feature of the provision and it is what makes a labour-supplying State's obligations meaningful.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between Regulation 4.2 and Regulation 4.5?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 4.2 is the SHIPOWNER's liability for sickness, injury or death occurring in connection with the seafarer's employment, running during and for a defined period after the engagement. Regulation 4.5 is the STATE's obligation to provide access to social security protection, and it reaches beyond the engagement into old age, invalidity and survivors' benefits. Standard A4.5 says the nine branches COMPLEMENT the protection under 4.1 and 4.2.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely answer 4.5 by describing 4.2, which loses the whole of the limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Were the 2022 MLC amendments in force at this sitting?

The operative text is the Convention as amended through the 2018 set, which entered into force 26 December 2020. Approved is not adopted is not in force.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How may a Member deliver the required social security protection?
retrieval_cards.answer: Through laws or regulations, private schemes, collective bargaining agreements, or a combination of these. Where coverage in a branch is inadequate the Member must give consideration to comparable benefits by other means, and Members must cooperate through bilateral or multilateral agreements to maintain rights acquired or in the course of acquisition regardless of residence. Each Member must also provide fair and effective procedures for the settlement of disputes.
retrieval_cards.why: Assuming legislation is the only route misses the flexibility that lets a mixed national system comply.

blocks.h: 1. The background - the gap the Convention was written to close

blocks.p: By the late 1990s the international regime for oil pollution was substantial but narrow. The 1992 CLC, backed by the 1992 Fund, applied only to persistent oil carried as cargo in bulk by a tanker. It said nothing about the far more common case of a bulk carrier, container ship or car carrier spilling its own fuel. A large modern non-tanker may carry several thousand tonnes of heavy fuel oil - more than the entire cargo of a small tanker - and a claimant faced with such a spill had no dedicated convention, no guaranteed insurer to sue and no certainty of recovery. The International Convention on Civil Liability for Bunker Oil Pollution Damage was adopted on 23 March 2001 and entered into force on 21 November 2008 to close exactly that gap.

blocks.h: 2. Its relevance - where it sits in the liability architecture

blocks.p: Its relevance is that it completes the map. Taken with CLC and the Fund for tanker cargo, and the HNS Convention for hazardous and noxious substances, the Bunkers Convention brings the fuel of essentially the whole world fleet inside a regime of strict liability, compulsory insurance and direct action against the insurer. It applies to pollution damage in the territory, territorial sea and exclusive economic zone of a State Party, and to preventive measures wherever taken. Its structural weakness, dealt with at step 7, is that it stops there: it creates no limitation fund of its own and no second tier of compensation.

Bunkers article 1.9 defines pollution damage as loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination resulting from the escape or discharge of bunker oil, provided that compensation for impairment of the environment other than loss of profit from that impairment is limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken; and it includes the costs of preventive measures and further loss or damage caused by preventive measures.

Against CLC 92: the definition is deliberately the same in substance. The drafters copied the CLC formula so that the two regimes would be interpreted consistently and no claimant would be better or worse off according to which convention applied. The difference lies not in what pollution damage means but in which oil, from which ship, triggers it.

Bunkers article 1.5: any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues of such oil. Three features matter. It expressly catches lubricating oil, which candidates routinely forget. It catches residues, so sludge and tank washings are within it. And unlike CLC it is not limited to persistent oil - a marine gas oil spill is bunker oil for these purposes.

Against CLC 92: CLC applies to persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil - crude, fuel oil, heavy diesel, lubricating oil - carried as cargo, and to such oil in the bunkers of a ship carrying that cargo. So the same drum of lubricating oil is CLC oil in a laden tanker's bunkers and Bunkers Convention oil in a bulk carrier's sump.

Bunkers article 8. Rights to compensation are extinguished unless an action is brought within three years from the date the damage occurred. In no case may an action be brought more than six years from the date of the incident which caused the damage. Where the incident consists of a series of occurrences, the six-year period runs from the date of the first occurrence.

Against CLC 92: substantially identical - CLC article VIII sets the same three-year and six-year periods on the same terms. This is one of the places where the drafters deliberately mirrored CLC. Note the wording: the right is extinguished, not merely barred, so it cannot be revived.
Three different things are commonly called exclusions and the answer should separate them:

ol: Excluded damage - the CLC carve-out. Article 4.1: the Convention does not apply to pollution damage as defined in the CLC, whether or not compensation is payable under it. This is the hinge that stops the two regimes overlapping. A laden tanker's bunker spill is a CLC matter, not a Bunkers matter.
Excluded ships. Article 4.2: it does not apply to warships, naval auxiliaries or other State-owned or operated ships used on government non-commercial service, unless a State Party decides otherwise.

The shipowner's defences - strictly not exclusions at all but a different route to no liability. Under article 3.3 the shipowner is not liable if the damage resulted from an act of war, hostilities, civil war, insurrection or a natural phenomenon of an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible character; was wholly caused by a third party's act or omission done with intent to cause damage; or was wholly caused by the negligence or wrongful act of a Government or authority responsible for maintaining lights or other navigational aids. Contributory fault of the claimant may also reduce or exonerate.

blocks.p: Against CLC 92: the defences are the same three, in the same terms. The excluded-ship provision is likewise mirrored. The CLC carve-out itself has no CLC equivalent, because CLC is the senior regime.

blocks.h: 7. How the Bunker Convention differs from CLC 92, taken together

rows: 'Shipowner' defined widely - registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, jointly and severally
No limit of its own. Article 6 preserves the right to limit under any applicable national or international regime, in practice the LLMC
Its own tonnage-based limits in article V
Registered owner of a ship over 1,000 GT
Ship carrying more than 2,000 tonnes of persistent oil as cargo

blocks.p: The practical consequence of rows three and four is the point worth making last: where a very large bunker spill exhausts the LLMC limit, there is nothing behind it. That is the principal criticism of the regime, and it is thrown into relief by the tanker regime examined at Q4 of this same paper - where CLC is backed by the 1992 Fund and, for States that have joined it, by the Supplementary Fund. The reason for the difference is not oversight but constituency: oil receivers could be identified and levied to build a fund for cargo, and there is no equivalent industry to levy for the fuel every ship burns.

The printed question gives you your own headings - (a), (b), (c), (d) - so the structure is free. The mark is lost in a different way: by defining the four terms and never doing the comparison the stem asks for. Every one of steps 3 to 6 therefore ends with an explicit 'Against CLC 92' sentence. That single habit converts a half answer into a full one.

Step 7 exists because the most important difference does not live under any of the four definitions. It is structural - who is liable, what limit applies, and what stands behind it. Putting it in a table at the end banks a large number of comparison marks quickly.

CLC is a cargo regime. Bunkers is a fuel regime. Everything else follows. CLC could afford exclusive channelling to the registered owner and a dedicated fund because the industry paying for the fund - oil receivers - is identifiable and finite. There is no equivalent constituency to levy for bunkers, so the Bunkers Convention got neither a fund nor its own limit, and had to widen the definition of 'shipowner' instead so that a claimant has more than one solvent defendant.

ul: Omitting lubricating oil from the definition of bunker oil. It is expressly in the text.
Saying bunker oil must be persistent. It need not be - that is a CLC requirement, not a Bunkers one.
Writing that liability is channelled to the registered owner. That is CLC. Under Bunkers it reaches the bareboat charterer, manager and operator as well.
Saying the Bunkers Convention has its own limits of liability. It does not - it borrows the LLMC.
Confusing the six-year long stop with the three-year period, or giving only one of the two.
Treating the shipowner's defences as if they were the article 4 exclusions. They are separate provisions doing separate work.
Forgetting the CLC carve-out - it is the single most important exclusion and the one that makes the system coherent.

'Whether or not compensation is payable under CLC.' Those words in article 4.1 matter. Even where the CLC claim fails, the Bunkers Convention does not step in. The claimant does not get a second bite.
The insurance thresholds are different units. Bunkers is 1,000 GT, a tonnage of the ship. CLC is 2,000 tonnes of oil carried, a quantity of cargo. Candidates frequently swap them.
'Extinguished', not 'barred'. The right ceases to exist.
Being asked what happens after the LLMC limit is exhausted on a bunker spill. The honest answer is that the convention regime provides nothing further.
Being asked whether the Bunkers Convention applies on the high seas. It applies to pollution damage in the territory, territorial sea and EEZ - but to preventive measures wherever taken.
A laden tanker spills bunkers. Which convention? CLC - and Bunkers is excluded by article 4.1.
A container ship spills lube oil. Which convention? Bunkers - lubricating oil is expressly within article 1.5.
Who can the claimant sue? Any of the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager or operator, jointly and severally; and the insurer directly.
Why is there no bunker fund? There is no identifiable cargo-receiving industry to levy, as there is for oil under the Fund Convention.
Is India a party? Yes, but write the answer on the Convention - the question asks about the Convention.

blocks.p: Two openers, four definitions, one table: 2-4-1. For the definitions use P-B-T-E - Pollution damage, Bunker oil, Time limits, Exclusions - which is the printed order, so nothing extra to remember. For the numbers, 3 and 6 are the time limits, 1,000 is Bunkers insurance in GT and 2,000 is CLC insurance in tonnes of cargo.

Compulsory insurance over 1,000 GT, direct action

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define bunker oil under the 2001 Convention.
retrieval_cards.answer: Any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues of such oil. It is not confined to persistent oil.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define pollution damage under the 2001 Convention.
retrieval_cards.answer: Loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination resulting from the escape or discharge of bunker oil, provided that compensation for environmental impairment other than loss of profit is limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken; and the costs of preventive measures and further loss or damage caused by preventive measures.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the time limits for claims, and what happens on a series of occurrences?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rights are extinguished unless action is brought within three years from the date the damage occurred, and in no case more than six years from the date of the incident. Where the incident consists of a series of occurrences, the six-year period runs from the date of the first occurrence.
retrieval_cards.why: Two periods, not one, plus the series rule. CLC article VIII is the same.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the exclusions, and how do they differ from the shipowner's defences?

The defences are separate - act of war or exceptional natural phenomenon, damage wholly caused by a third party intending damage, or wholly caused by the negligence of an authority responsible for navigational aids.
retrieval_cards.why: Three different things get called 'exclusions'. Separating them is what a good answer does.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the four structural differences between the Bunkers Convention and CLC 92.
retrieval_cards.answer: Who is liable - Bunkers reaches registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator jointly and severally; CLC channels exclusively to the registered owner. Limitation - Bunkers has none of its own and preserves the LLMC; CLC has its own limits. Second tier - Bunkers has no fund; CLC has the 1992 Fund and Supplementary Fund. retrieval_cards.why: This is the comparison the stem actually asks for and the largest single block of marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A laden tanker spills its own bunkers. Which convention applies?
retrieval_cards.answer: CLC 92. Bunkers article 4.1 excludes pollution damage as defined in the CLC, whether or not compensation is actually payable under it - so the claimant cannot fall back on the Bunkers Convention if the CLC claim fails.
retrieval_cards.why: The classic viva question, and the 'whether or not payable' wording is the sting.

blocks.h: 1. a) What GISIS is, and the problem it solves

blocks.p: The Global Integrated Shipping Information System is the IMO Secretariat's web-based platform for the information that Member States are required or invited to report under IMO instruments. Before it, that information arrived as paper circulars and correspondence: it was slow, inconsistently formatted, effectively unsearchable, and once filed it was of little use to anyone. Conventions imposed reporting duties without creating anywhere useful for the reports to go.

GISIS turns those duties into a single, structured, electronic repository. Its purpose is threefold - to collect what States must report, to disseminate it to those who need it, and to make it analysable so that the Organization can see patterns rather than incidents.

blocks.h: 2. a) The components - the module structure

blocks.p: GISIS is organised into modules, each corresponding to a reporting obligation or an information need. The principal ones include:

ul: Marine casualties and incidents - casualty reports and investigation reports;
Piracy and armed robbery against ships;
Port reception facilities - what exists at each port, and reports of alleged inadequacy;
Contact points - the national focal points a State must designate;
Ship and company particulars, built on the IMO identification number schemes;
Recognized organizations - which ROs each flag has authorized, and for what;
Status of multilateral conventions - who is party to what, and from when;
Port State control, and survey and certification;
Marine environment and MARPOL reporting, including fuel oil availability;
Maritime security and the condition assessment scheme.

blocks.p: The list is not exhaustive, and it should not be memorised as though it were fixed: modules are added and reorganised administratively as reporting needs change, without any instrument being amended.

blocks.h: 3. a) Access, and how the data gets in

blocks.p: Content is divided between public and restricted. Much is openly accessible after free registration - convention status, ship particulars, recognized organizations, reception facility details - while operationally or commercially sensitive material is confined to Member State users. Data is entered and maintained by each State's designated focal points, with the Secretariat administering the system rather than authoring the content.
That division of labour is the system's strength and its weakness together: the data is authoritative because the reporting State owns it, and it is incomplete wherever a State does not report.

blocks.h: 4. a) How it facilitates data sharing among Member States

ul: One repository, one format. A State reports once, electronically, in a defined structure, instead of circulating documents bilaterally.
Immediacy. What is entered is visible at once, rather than after a publication cycle.

Searchable and analysable. Data can be filtered, aggregated and exported, which is what allows the Organization's own sub-committees to analyse casualties and identify systemic causes rather than reading individual reports.
It feeds regulatory work. Casualty analysis informs amendments; port State control data supports targeting; convention status underpins every enforcement decision a port State takes.

Transparency and accountability. Because the record is visible, a State's failure to report is visible too - which is itself a compliance mechanism, and is used in the Organization's member State audit work.
It directs assistance. Gaps revealed by the data show the Organization where technical cooperation and capacity building are actually needed.

blocks.h: 5. b) Reporting on compliant fuel oil

blocks.p: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 18, 'Fuel oil availability and quality', is the hook. It sits behind the sulphur limits - 0.50% m/m globally since 1 January 2020 and 0.10% m/m in emission control areas - and it does two things that reach the Organization.

ul: Parties must promote the availability of compliant fuel oil and inform the Organization about it, including where it is and is not obtainable. That is what makes a global limit administrable.

Where a ship cannot obtain compliant fuel oil despite best efforts, it records the fact in a fuel oil non-availability report, notifying its Administration and the competent authority of the port of destination, and the information reaches the Organization.

blocks.p: GISIS is where those two streams are collected and made visible. The value is that an individual non-availability report is an excuse, but many reports naming the same port is evidence of a supply failure - and only a central register can convert one into the other. It also protects the honest operator: a port State officer can see whether non-availability at that port is corroborated, and the shipowner is not left arguing an unverifiable case.

blocks.h: 6. b) Reporting inadequacy of port reception facilities

blocks.p: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 17, 'Reception facilities', and its counterparts in the other Annexes, require Parties to ensure the provision of adequate reception facilities. The port reception facilities module serves that obligation from both ends.

ul: It holds a database of the facilities available at each port - waste types accepted, capacities and contacts - so that a ship can plan its discharges before arrival rather than discovering the position alongside.

It carries the alleged inadequacy reporting mechanism. Where a facility is unavailable, insufficient, unreasonably delayed or effectively inaccessible, the master reports the alleged inadequacy; the report goes to the flag Administration, which forwards it to the port State and to the Organization; and the port State is expected to investigate and respond, with the exchange recorded.

blocks.p: The word alleged is deliberate and is worth noticing: the system records a claim and a response, not a finding. It is a structured complaint channel, not an adjudication.

blocks.h: 7. b) What the reported data is actually useful for

blocks.p: Both limbs of the printed question turn on one idea. A prohibition addressed to the ship is only enforceable, and only fair, if the shore side delivers. A ship may be required to burn compliant fuel only if compliant fuel can be bought; a ship may be prohibited from discharging waste at sea only if there is somewhere ashore to land it. In each case the obligation on the shipowner is matched by an obligation on States - to promote fuel availability, and to provide adequate reception facilities - and GISIS is the feedback channel that shows whether those State-side obligations are being met.

So the usefulness runs at four levels. For the ship, it is operational: plan the waste discharge and the bunkering with knowledge of what is actually there. For the company, it is evidential: a documented report is the defence against a deficiency, and it is what turns a commercial dispute into a regulatory record. For the port and flag States, it creates an obligation that can be seen to be discharged or not. And for the Organization, aggregation is the whole point - it converts scattered individual complaints into evidence of a systemic shortage at a named port or in a named region, which is what justifies technical cooperation, guidance or, in the end, an amendment. Its limitation follows from the same design: GISIS reports only what is reported, so under-reporting appears in the data as compliance.

Limb (a) has two demands - the key functions and components, and how it facilitates data sharing. Give the modules as a list, because a list of modules is counted, and then give the data-sharing benefits as a second list. Two lists, eight marks, no prose padding.

Limb (b) is where candidates lose marks, because it looks like a request for opinion and is actually a request for two specific reporting mechanisms. Name the regulation behind each - regulation 18 for fuel oil and regulation 17 for reception facilities - describe the workflow, and only then discuss usefulness. Step 7 is the discussion, and it is what lifts the limb above description.

blocks.h: The printed question has a looseness worth handling deliberately

blocks.p: Limb (b) says 'this module', in the singular, and then asks about two different things - compliant fuel oil, and inadequacy of port reception facilities. These are handled in different parts of GISIS: fuel oil availability sits with the MARPOL and marine environment reporting, and reception facilities have their own module. Do not try to force them into one. Answer both, and note in a clause that they are separate reporting streams serving the same purpose. Recognising the looseness and dealing with it cleanly reads as competence, not pedantry.

blocks.h: The one idea that unifies limb (b)

blocks.p: Every obligation MARPOL places on the ship has a matching obligation on the State, and GISIS is how you find out whether the State kept its side.

ul: The ship must burn compliant fuel - so Parties must promote its availability, and non-availability must be reportable.
The ship must not discharge waste at sea - so Parties must provide adequate reception facilities, and inadequacy must be reportable.

blocks.p: State that once and the whole of limb (b) becomes an argument rather than two descriptions. It is also the honest answer to 'why does the Organization bother collecting this?'

ul: Describing GISIS as a ship-tracking or AIS-type system. It is a reporting and information system, not an operational traffic picture.
Saying it is entirely public. It is mixed - some modules open after free registration, others restricted to Member State users.
Saying IMO writes the content. Member States enter it through designated focal points; the Secretariat administers the platform.
Reciting a memorised list of modules as though it were fixed and complete. The set changes administratively, and saying so is safer and more accurate than a confident wrong list.
Answering limb (b) without naming a single regulation. Regulation 18 for fuel oil availability and quality, regulation 17 for reception facilities - both MARPOL Annex VI, chapter 3.

Treating a non-availability report as a waiver or exemption. It is a report of fact made after best efforts; it does not authorise burning non-compliant fuel as a matter of course, and it invites scrutiny rather than ending it.
Forgetting that a reception facility report is of an ALLEGED inadequacy, and that the port State is expected to respond.
Who enters the data? The Member State's designated focal point - not IMO, and not the ship.
What is the sulphur limit that makes fuel availability an issue? 0.50% m/m globally from 1 January 2020, and 0.10% m/m in emission control areas.

Where does a non-availability report go? To the ship's Administration and to the competent authority of the port of destination - and from there onward to the Organization. Not to IMO directly from the ship.
Who reports an inadequate reception facility, and to whom? The master, through the flag Administration, which forwards to the port State and the Organization.
Does GISIS decide anything? No. It records claims, responses and reported facts. It is not an adjudicating body.
What is its principal weakness? It reflects only what States report, so a gap in the data can mean either that there is no problem or that nobody reported one - and those are not the same thing.

questions.understand_first: Every IMO convention creates reporting duties - tell the Organization about your casualties, your recognized organizations, your reception facilities, your fuel supply. For decades those reports arrived as paper, in whatever format the sending State chose, and once filed they were almost useless: nobody could search them, aggregate them or see a pattern in them. GISIS exists to fix that, and it is best understood not as a website but as the Organization's memory. That framing answers limb (a) - the modules are simply one drawer per reporting duty, filled by the States themselves and administered rather than authored by the Secretariat. It also answers limb (b), which is really a question about why anyone would want this data. The answer is that MARPOL works by prohibiting things on board - do not burn high-sulphur fuel, do not discharge waste at sea - and each of those prohibitions is only workable if the shore side provides an alternative. So each is paired with a duty on States, to promote compliant fuel and to provide adequate reception facilities. GISIS is where a ship reports that the shore side failed, and where enough such reports become evidence that a port has a real problem.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which MARPOL Annex VI regulations sit behind the two reporting streams in limb (b)?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 18, fuel oil availability and quality, for compliant fuel - Parties must promote availability and inform the Organization, and a ship unable to obtain compliant fuel files a non-availability report. Regulation 17, reception facilities, for port waste - Parties must ensure adequate reception facilities, and alleged inadequacy is reportable. Both are in chapter 3 of Annex VI.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming the two regulations is what turns limb (b) from a discussion of a website into a regulatory answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You cannot obtain compliant fuel oil at your next bunker port. What is the mechanism?
retrieval_cards.answer: Having made best efforts to obtain compliant fuel, you record the fact in a fuel oil non-availability report and notify your Administration and the competent authority of the relevant port of destination; the information reaches the Organization and is collected centrally. It is a report of fact, not a waiver or an exemption - it does not authorise burning non-compliant fuel as a matter of course and it invites scrutiny rather than ending it.
retrieval_cards.why: The 'it is not a waiver' point is the discriminating one, and it is a standard oral follow-up.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The port's reception facility cannot take your sludge. What is the reporting chain?
retrieval_cards.answer: The master reports the alleged inadequacy; the report goes to the flag Administration, which forwards it to the port State and to the Organization; and the port State is expected to investigate and respond, with the exchange recorded in the GISIS port reception facilities module. The report is of an ALLEGED inadequacy - the system records a claim and a response, not a finding.
retrieval_cards.why: The chain has four parties in a fixed order, and the word 'alleged' is what candidates miss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does the Organization collect this data at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because a prohibition addressed to the ship is enforceable and fair only if the shore side delivers. A ship can be required to burn compliant fuel only if compliant fuel can be bought, and can be prohibited from discharging waste at sea only if there is somewhere to land it. Each duty on the shipowner is matched by a duty on States, and GISIS is the feedback channel showing whether those duties are being met - aggregation turns individual complaints into evidence of a systemic shortage at a named port.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the argument that unifies limb (b) and lifts it from description to discussion.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the principal weakness of GISIS as an information source?
retrieval_cards.answer: It reflects only what States actually report. A gap in the data may mean there is no problem, or it may mean nobody reported one, and the system cannot distinguish the two. Its authority comes from the reporting State owning the entry, and its incompleteness comes from exactly the same place.
retrieval_cards.why: Any question inviting evaluation needs a limitation, and this one follows directly from the system's design rather than being a generic criticism.

blocks.h: 1. a) The Convention - what it does and why

blocks.p: The International Convention on the Control of Harmful Anti-fouling Systems on Ships, 2001 - the AFS Convention - entered into force on 17 September 2008. Its purpose is to prohibit or restrict anti-fouling systems that are harmful to the marine environment while allowing ships to continue to control fouling.

It exists because of organotin compounds, principally tributyl tin. TBT was an outstandingly effective antifouling biocide and an outstandingly damaging pollutant: it persists, it accumulates in sediment and in the food chain, and it causes imposex and shell deformity in shellfish at concentrations of a few parts per trillion, with severe damage recorded around ports and shellfish grounds.

The Convention applies to ships entitled to fly the flag of a Party and to ships operating under a Party's authority. The substances actually controlled are listed in Annex 1, and that list can be added to by amendment - which is exactly what has since happened. Compliance is enforced through survey and certification and through inspection by port State officers, who may examine the certificate or declaration and may take a sample of the coating.
Organotin compounds acting as biocides in anti-fouling systems:

ul: no ship may apply or re-apply them - effective 1 January 2003;
from 1 January 2008 a ship must either not bear such a system, or must carry a coating that forms a barrier to it leaching from the underlying non-compliant system.

blocks.p: Cybutryne was added to Annex 1 by amendment adopted on 17 June 2021, which entered into force on 1 January 2023. It was therefore fully in force at the date of this paper, and an answer that describes only the tin position is incomplete.

ul: All ships: no application or re-application of an anti-fouling system containing cybutryne, from 1 January 2023.

Ships already bearing cybutryne in the external coating layer on that date must either remove the system or apply a coating forming a barrier to it leaching - at the next scheduled renewal of the anti-fouling system after 1 January 2023, and no later than 60 months after the last application of a cybutryne-containing system.

Limited exclusions apply, including fixed and floating platforms, FSUs and FPSOs constructed before that date which have not since been in dry dock, ships not engaged on international voyages, and ships under 400 GT on international voyages where the coastal State accepts it.

blocks.p: The practical lesson is that 'tin-free' does not mean 'unregulated'. Cybutryne was a common booster biocide in tin-free paints, so the second wave of control fell on the very coatings that replaced TBT.

blocks.h: 3. a) Documents and records to demonstrate compliance

blocks.p: What a surveyor or port State control officer will expect to be produced:

ul: International Anti-Fouling System Certificate (IAFS Certificate) - for ships of 400 gross tonnage and above engaged in international voyages, issued by or on behalf of the Administration after the required survey.

The Record of Anti-Fouling Systems - attached to and forming part of the certificate. It records the system applied, the facility that applied it and the date, and which compliance option applies to each controlled substance: never applied, applied and since removed, applied and covered with a sealer coat, or not in the external coating layer.
Declaration on Anti-Fouling System - for ships of 24 metres or more in length but less than 400 gross tonnage engaged in international voyages, signed by the owner or the owner's authorized agent.
Supporting documentation for that Declaration - a paint receipt or contractor's invoice, or equivalent evidence of what was applied.

Manufacturer's technical documentation - product data sheets and declarations confirming the composition of the system and the absence of controlled substances, together with application records: product, batch, area, dry film thickness and dates.
Survey records and reports - of the initial survey, and of any survey carried out when the anti-fouling system is changed or replaced, with the certificate endorsed or reissued accordingly.
Record of any sealer or barrier coat applied over a non-compliant system, naming the facility and the date, since that is what the certificate itself must state.
Dry-docking and planned maintenance records evidencing the last application and the next scheduled renewal - these establish the 60-month position for cybutryne.

blocks.p: One point specific to this period: since the cybutryne amendment the certificate must be in the amended model form, which carries cybutryne as well as organotins. Affected ships were given a transitional period to obtain a certificate in that form, and that transition was still running at the date of this paper.

A soluble matrix coating, traditionally rosin-based. Seawater slowly dissolves the binder, and as it dissolves it releases the biocide dispersed within it - essentially a refinement of the old soluble-matrix paints.

Because release depends on physical dissolution rather than a controlled chemical reaction, the release rate is not well regulated and tails off with time, and a thick, uneven leached layer builds up on the hull. That layer increases roughness and drag, so fuel performance degrades over the docking cycle. It is the cheapest of the four, easy to apply and easy to overcoat, and is generally suited to shorter drydock intervals and lower-activity ships.

The important difference is chemical. The biocide is chemically bonded into an acrylic copolymer backbone rather than merely mixed into a soluble binder. In seawater the surface layer hydrolyses, releasing the biocide at a controlled, near-linear rate, and the spent binder then becomes soluble and erodes away - so the coating polishes itself smooth as it works.

The consequences are a thin and stable leached layer, a predictable release rate that can be engineered to the ship's speed and activity, longer service life - commonly to a full five-year docking cycle - and better sustained hydrodynamic performance because the surface stays smooth. It costs more than CDP. Modern tin-free SPCs use copper, zinc or silyl acrylate chemistries in place of the original tin ones.
A blend of the two technologies above - rosin and copolymer chemistry combined in one binder - intended to capture some of the controlled polishing behaviour of SPC at closer to CDP cost.

The result is intermediate on every axis: more predictable release and less leached-layer build-up than pure CDP, but less precisely controlled than a true SPC; intermediate service life; intermediate price. It is a sensible compromise for moderate trading patterns and medium docking intervals. Note that 'hybrid' is a commercial label rather than a defined term, and formulations sold under it vary considerably.

These are fundamentally different: they contain no biocide at all and work by physics rather than by poisoning. A silicone or fluoropolymer elastomer gives a surface of very low surface energy and very high smoothness, to which fouling organisms cannot attach firmly. Such growth as does settle is sheared off by the water flow once the ship is moving.

Strengths: the lowest drag of any of the four, hence the best fuel performance, and no biocide released into the sea, which is the strongest environmental position. Limitations are real: performance depends on regular activity and adequate speed, so the ship fouls during prolonged idle periods or slow steaming; the film is mechanically soft and easily damaged and is difficult to repair; it requires a full tie-coat system and careful surface preparation; and it carries the highest initial cost.

The choice follows the ship's trading pattern, service speed, proportion of idle time and intended drydock interval. A fast, regularly operating ship on a five-year cycle rewards a fouling release or a good SPC; a slower ship with irregular employment and long port stays is better served by a biocidal SPC or hybrid; CDP remains defensible where the docking interval is short and first cost dominates. Whatever is selected must be free of the substances controlled under Annex 1 - now including cybutryne - and must be documented so that compliance can be demonstrated.

Limb (a) contains a trap of drafting. It says 'briefly discuss' the Convention and then 'state ALL documents and records'. The word all converts the second half into a checklist, and a checklist is marked by counting items. So the discussion is kept genuinely brief and the documents are written as an explicit list, one line each. A flowing paragraph that mentions the certificate in passing will lose marks that a list would have collected.

Limb (b) names four technologies at two marks each. Each is given mechanism, performance and limitation in that order. Step 8 is not asked for explicitly, but 'discuss various alternatives' invites a comparison, and a short selection paragraph is what distinguishes an engineer's answer from a paint catalogue.

Cybutryne controls entered into force on 1 January 2023 - twenty months before this sitting. Much of the study material on this topic was written when the AFS Convention meant TBT and nothing else, and an answer built from that material describes only the tin position and is incomplete for September 2024. This is worth internalising as a general point: an old paper's correct answer is not always the old answer.

Two further details are specific to this sitting. The 60-month rule was live - ships bearing cybutryne had to remove it or seal it over at the next scheduled renewal after 1 January 2023 and no later than 60 months after the last application. And the transitional period for obtaining a certificate in the amended form was still running, so at this date a ship could legitimately still hold a certificate in the older form.

blocks.h: The one idea that organises limb (b)

blocks.p: There are only two ways to keep a hull clean, and the four named products are variations on them. Either you release a biocide, or you make the surface impossible to grip.

ul: Release a biocide - and then the only question is how well you control the release. CDP dissolves and controls it poorly. SPC hydrolyses and controls it well. Hybrid sits between them. That single axis explains cost, service life, leached-layer thickness and drag for all three.
Make the surface impossible to grip - fouling release. No biocide, lowest drag, but it depends on the ship moving, and the film is soft and expensive.

blocks.p: If you can state that framing in one sentence at the start of limb (b), the four descriptions write themselves and you will not confuse CDP with SPC, which is the commonest error in this topic.

ul: Answering the Convention as a TBT-only instrument. Cybutryne was controlled from 1 January 2023 and was in force at this sitting.
Giving the certificate but forgetting the Record of Anti-Fouling Systems, which is attached to and forms part of it, and the Declaration for the ship between 24 m and 400 GT.
Confusing CDP and SPC. CDP dissolves; SPC hydrolyses and polishes. The biocide is mixed into a CDP binder and chemically bound into an SPC backbone.
Calling fouling release paint an antifouling in the biocidal sense. It contains no biocide; that is its defining feature.
Presenting fouling release as simply the best option. It needs the ship to move, and it is soft, costly and hard to repair.
Writing the organotin dates the wrong way round. 1 January 2003 is when application stopped; 1 January 2008 is when ships had to stop bearing it or seal it over.
Treating 'briefly discuss' as permission to write half the answer on the history of TBT.
'All documents and records'. The examiner is counting. Include the Record, the Declaration, the supporting paint documentation and the survey records - not just the certificate.
Remove OR seal. For both organotins and cybutryne the requirement is a choice: remove the system, or apply a coating forming a barrier over it. Candidates routinely give only removal.
The tonnage and length thresholds. 400 GT and above gets a certificate; 24 m or more but under 400 GT gets a declaration. Expect to be asked what a 30 m, 300 GT ship carries.
Who signs the Declaration. The owner or the owner's authorized agent - not the master, and not a surveyor.
The 60-month rule. It is not a flat deadline: it is the next scheduled renewal after 1 January 2023, subject to an outer limit of 60 months from the last application.
Port State sampling. An officer may do more than read the certificate - a sample of the coating may be taken.

questions.understand_first: Fouling costs fuel, so ships are painted with something that stops marine growth. For decades that something was tributyl tin, which worked extremely well and turned out to be one of the most damaging substances ever deliberately released into the sea - it deforms shellfish at concentrations measured in parts per trillion. The AFS Convention exists to ban that class of substance and to make a ship prove, on paper, what is actually on her hull. So limb (a) is really two questions: what the Convention prohibits, and what a surveyor or port State officer will ask you to produce. Limb (b) is the engineering consequence - once tin is gone, how else can a coating keep a hull clean? There are only two ideas: keep releasing a biocide in a controlled way, or make the surface so slippery that nothing can hold on. The four named paint types are variations on those two ideas.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the AFS Convention control, and when did it enter into force?
retrieval_cards.answer: The International Convention on the Control of Harmful Anti-fouling Systems on Ships, 2001, in force 17 September 2008. It prohibits or restricts anti-fouling systems harmful to the marine environment, listing the controlled substances in Annex 1, and enforces this through survey and certification and port State inspection.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the organotin control dates and what each requires.
retrieval_cards.answer: From 1 January 2003 no ship may apply or re-apply organotin compounds acting as biocides. From 1 January 2008 a ship must either not bear such a system, or must carry a coating forming a barrier to it leaching from the underlying non-compliant system.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the position on cybutryne, and why does it matter for this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Cybutryne was added to Annex 1 by MEPC.331(76), adopted 17 June 2021 and in force 1 January 2023 - twenty months before this examination. No ship may apply or re-apply it. A ship already bearing it must remove it or apply a barrier coating at the next scheduled renewal after 1 January 2023, and no later than 60 months after the last application. A tin-only answer is incomplete.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the documents and records demonstrating AFS compliance.
retrieval_cards.answer: IAFS Certificate for ships of 400 GT and above on international voyages, with the Record of Anti-Fouling Systems attached to and forming part of it; a Declaration on Anti-Fouling System for ships 24 m or more but under 400 GT, signed by the owner or authorized agent and supported by a paint receipt or contractor invoice; manufacturer data sheets and application records; survey records for the initial survey and on change or replacement; the record of any sealer coat with facility and date; and dry-docking records.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a controlled depletion polymer differ from a self-polishing copolymer?
retrieval_cards.answer: In CDP the biocide is mixed into a soluble rosin-based binder which dissolves in seawater - release is poorly controlled, tails off with time, and a thick uneven leached layer builds up, raising drag. In SPC the biocide is chemically bound into an acrylic copolymer backbone; the surface hydrolyses at a controlled near-linear rate and the spent binder erodes, so the coating polishes itself smooth and keeps a thin stable leached layer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a hybrid TBT-free paint?
retrieval_cards.answer: A blend of rosin and copolymer technologies in one binder, giving behaviour between CDP and SPC - more predictable release and less leached-layer build-up than CDP, less precise control than a true SPC, with intermediate cost and service life. The term is a commercial label rather than a defined one, so formulations vary.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a fouling release coating work, and what are its limitations?
retrieval_cards.answer: It contains no biocide. A silicone or fluoropolymer elastomer gives a very low surface energy and extremely smooth surface that fouling cannot grip, and growth is sheared off by water flow once the ship moves. It gives the lowest drag and releases no biocide, but it depends on regular activity and adequate speed, is mechanically soft and easily damaged, needs a full tie-coat system, and has the highest first cost.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is recorded in the Record of Anti-Fouling Systems?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is attached to and forms part of the IAFS Certificate. It records the anti-fouling system applied, the facility that applied it and the date, and for each controlled substance which compliance option applies - never applied, applied and since removed, applied and covered with a sealer coat, or not present in the external coating layer.

blocks.h: 1. Where the energy to be recovered is

blocks.p: A screw propeller working behind a hull typically converts only about 65 to 72 per cent of delivered power into useful thrust. The losses are of three kinds: axial, in the sternward momentum of the race; rotational, in the swirl the blades impart to it; and frictional and vortex losses, principally the hub vortex shed from the boss. The rotational component alone is commonly of the order of 8 to 12 per cent of delivered power on a single-screw merchant ship.

The rudder is the only large body standing in that race. It is therefore both an opportunity - the swirl arrives at it already rotating, so a correctly oriented surface there sees an angle of attack for nothing - and a liability, because a plain rudder behind a bare boss adds drag and lets the hub vortex run on unchecked. The four devices below exploit the first and reduce the second.

A rudder thrust fin is a horizontal foil, usually fitted as a pair port and starboard, mounted on the rudder at or near the level of the propeller shaft, inside the slipstream. Because the race is rotating, the flow arrives at the fin with a tangential component: upward on one side of the shaft and downward on the other. Each fin is set at the angle that turns that oncoming flow into lift, and because the flow is inclined, the lift vector is tilted forward. Its horizontal component is thrust, generated with no additional power.

ul: The two fins are set at different angles, or in mirror image, because the swirl direction differs above and below the shaft.
Gains quoted in industry literature are typically of the order of 2 to 5 per cent in delivered power, and are strongly dependent on span, chord and angle of attack.
The angle is fixed at build. The device is optimised for one draught and speed and gives less, or in extreme off-design conditions nothing, elsewhere.
It is a source of added appendage drag when not loaded, and a candidate for cavitation erosion if it sits too close to the blade tips.

blocks.p: Here the recovery is built into the rudder itself rather than added to it. On a single-screw ship the propeller turns one way, so the race strikes the upper half of the rudder from one side and the lower half from the other. A conventional symmetrical rudder, aligned with the centreline, therefore meets the flow at an angle of attack of the wrong sign over half its span, producing side force, drag and early cavitation.

An asymmetric rudder cures this by making the two halves different. In the developed form - the twisted leading edge rudder - the leading edge is twisted in opposite directions above and below the shaft line, so that each half is aligned with the swirl it actually meets.

ul: The rudder becomes a swirl-recovery surface: the side force on the two halves is turned into a net forward component.
It reduces drag and cavitation, and with it rudder erosion and propeller-excited vibration.
It is handed - built for one direction of rotation - so it is a design decision, not a universal retrofit.
Because it changes the rudder body rather than adding to it, it carries no added appendage and its benefit degrades more gracefully off design than a fixed fin.

blocks.p: The propeller boss sheds a strong hub vortex, and behind a bare boss the flow separates, leaving a low-pressure wake that pulls the ship astern. A rudder bulb is a streamlined body of revolution fitted to the rudder leading edge, coaxial with the shaft and sized and positioned so that it forms an almost continuous body with the propeller hub cap, closing the gap between them.

ul: It suppresses or displaces the hub vortex, removing a pure loss.
It restores pressure behind the boss by giving the flow a body to close around instead of separating, which is a genuine reduction in resistance rather than a recovery of energy.
The diameter and the axial gap govern the result; too large or too far aft and the bulb adds more drag than it saves.
It is most often fitted together with fins, the bulb conditioning the flow the fins work in, so the two are designed as one installation and their savings are not simply additive.

blocks.p: The vane wheel, patented by Otto Grim in 1966, is the most ambitious of the four and the only one that moves. It is a freely rotating bladed wheel mounted on the shaft line immediately aft of the propeller, of larger diameter than the propeller, with no mechanical connection to it or to the shaft. It runs at its own speed, typically around a third to a half of propeller revolutions, driven entirely by the water.
Its cleverness is that one blade does two jobs at different radii:

ol: The inner portion, standing inside the propeller race, works as a turbine. It extracts energy from the swirl and axial velocity of the slipstream, and that is what drives the wheel round.

The outer portion, standing outside the race in undisturbed water, works as a propeller. Driven by the torque the inner part has extracted, it produces additional thrust over a larger disc area and therefore at higher efficiency.

blocks.p: The wheel thus takes wasted energy from a small, fast, disturbed stream and returns it as thrust in a large, slow, clean one. Gains of the order of 5 to 10 per cent were claimed and some were demonstrated. In service the device proved difficult: the long, thin, unsupported blades of the outer portion are fatigue-loaded and blade loss and shedding occurred; performance falls away in a seaway and off design, when the wheel can windmill unhelpfully; and it adds a rotating component aft of the propeller with its own bearing and clearance problems. It is now of more importance as a principle - and as an examination question - than as a device in general service.

blocks.h: 6. Whether a claimed gain is real on this ship

blocks.p: All four claims are hull-specific. A device recovers only what the propeller behind that hull actually wastes, so the gain depends on the wake field, block coefficient, propeller loading, draught and service speed. Three consequences follow, and they are where the marks are at this level. First, a quoted percentage means nothing without the condition it was measured in, and model-scale results require a scale-effect correction before they can be believed at full scale. Second, devices interact: a bulb changes the flow the fins see, so savings must be assessed for the installation as a whole. Third, the real case is the operating profile - a ship that spends its life slow-steaming at part draught will not realise a gain optimised for design condition, and the payback calculation must be built on the actual profile, on class approval of the attachment and its structure, and on the effect on manoeuvring, which a rudder-mounted device necessarily touches.

The examiner has done the structuring for you. Four devices are named and each carries 4 marks, so the answer is four equal blocks and nothing else can be substituted for them. The single most common way to lose marks here is to write a good general essay on energy-saving devices - pre-swirl stators, ducts, propeller boss cap fins, air lubrication - none of which is asked for. Answer the four printed limbs.

blocks.h: The one idea that unlocks all four

blocks.p: Rotational loss. The propeller leaves the race spinning, and that spin is energy already paid for and thrown away. Two of these devices recover it - the fin and the twisted rudder turn swirl into forward force, and the vane wheel takes it mechanically. Two stop further waste - the bulb removes the hub vortex and the separation behind the boss. If you can say which of the two categories a device is in, you can reconstruct its explanation from first principles.

blocks.h: Keep recovery and drag reduction apart

ul: Recovery - thrust fins, asymmetric and twisted rudders, vane wheels. They convert energy already in the water into thrust.
Drag and vortex reduction - rudder bulbs. They do not recover anything; they stop a loss from happening.

The bulb is often described loosely as recovering hub-vortex energy. The defensible statement is that it suppresses the vortex and restores pressure behind the boss. Say that and the point is safe either way.
Describing an asymmetric rudder as a rudder offset to one side of the centreline. The asymmetry is in the section and the twist about the shaft line, matching the opposite swirl above and below.
Saying the Grim vane wheel is geared to or driven by the shaft. It is entirely free-running; there is no mechanical connection, and that is the whole point.
Making the vane wheel the same diameter as the propeller. It is larger, and it must be, because the outer portion has to stand outside the race to act as a propeller.
Quoting a saving as a hard number. Every figure is conditional on the hull and the operating condition.
Adding the percentages of several devices together.
Ignoring manoeuvring. Anything bolted to a rudder changes the way she steers, and class will want to see the structure.

"Currently in use" in the stem. The Grim vane wheel is the odd one out - historically important, largely not in service. Say so rather than pretending it is common; an answer that quietly treats all four as current practice is weaker, not stronger.
Limb (d) is worth the same 4 marks as the others even though it is the least used. Do not short it.
The stem says the devices contribute to propulsion effectiveness, not to steering. Manoeuvring belongs in the closing judgement, not in place of the hydrodynamics.

questions.understand_first: A propeller does not convert all the power it is given into useful thrust. Some of what it leaves behind is axial - water thrown astern faster than it needs to be - and some is rotational: the race leaves the disc spinning, and that spin is wasted energy. Behind the propeller of a single-screw ship sits a large flat object in exactly that spinning race: the rudder. Every device in this question does one of two things with it - it either recovers some of the rotational energy and turns it into forward thrust, or it stops wasting more, by removing a vortex or a separation the rudder itself creates. Read the four limbs that way and they stop being four unrelated gadgets.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the rudder-efficiency question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Where the losses are - then the four printed limbs in order: (a) thrust fins, (b) asymmetric and twisted rudders, (c) rudder bulbs, (d) Grim vane wheels - then the management judgement on whether a claimed gain is real on this ship.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner prints 4 + 4 + 4 + 4. The four blocks must be equal, and the surrounding material has to be paid for out of the same 16 marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the rotational loss, and why does it matter here?
retrieval_cards.answer: The propeller leaves its race spinning as well as moving astern. That swirl is energy already paid for and thrown away - of the order of 8 to 12 per cent of delivered power on a single-screw ship. The rudder stands directly in it, which is why the rudder region is where these devices work.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the single idea behind all four devices. Knowing it lets you reconstruct any of them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a rudder thrust fin produce thrust without power?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is a horizontal foil on the rudder inside the propeller race. The race is rotating, so the flow meets the fin at an angle of attack without the fin being turned. The fin develops lift, and because the oncoming flow is inclined the lift vector tilts forward; its horizontal component is thrust.
retrieval_cards.why: The mechanism is the mark. Describing the fin's shape without the inclined-lift argument earns very little.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What exactly is asymmetric about an asymmetric rudder?
retrieval_cards.answer: The section and the twist about the shaft line, not the position. The propeller race strikes the upper half of the rudder from one side and the lower half from the other, so the leading edge is twisted in opposite senses above and below the shaft to align each half with the swirl it actually meets.
retrieval_cards.why: The commonest error is to describe a rudder offset to one side of the centreline. That is a different thing entirely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does a rudder bulb recover energy or reduce loss?
retrieval_cards.answer: Properly, it reduces loss. It suppresses the hub vortex and gives the flow a body to close around instead of separating behind a bare boss, restoring pressure there. It is often described loosely as recovering hub-vortex energy; the safe formulation is suppression and pressure recovery.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the one device in the four that is not a recovery device, and saying so shows you understand the mechanism rather than the marketing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain how a Grim vane wheel works.
retrieval_cards.answer: It is a freely rotating wheel aft of and coaxial with the propeller, larger in diameter, with no mechanical connection to the shaft. Its inner portion stands inside the propeller race and acts as a turbine, extracting energy from the swirl and driving the wheel round; its outer portion stands outside the race in clean water and acts as a propeller, converting that energy into additional thrust over a larger disc.
retrieval_cards.why: One blade doing two jobs at two radii is the whole idea, and it is what distinguishes the vane wheel from every other device on the list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must a vane wheel be larger in diameter than the propeller?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because its outer portion has to stand outside the propeller race to work as a propeller in undisturbed water. If the wheel were the same diameter, the whole blade would sit in the slipstream and there would be no propeller portion to return the extracted energy as thrust.
retrieval_cards.why: A favourite oral follow-up, and it tests whether the turbine-plus-propeller split has actually been understood.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A maker offers a 4 per cent saving from a rudder thrust fin. What do you ask before agreeing?
retrieval_cards.answer: In what condition was the 4 per cent measured - draught, speed, loading - and was it model scale or full scale, with what scale correction? How does it behave at our actual operating profile rather than at the design point? What else is already fitted, since devices interact and savings do not simply add? What does class require for the attachment and its structure, and what is the effect on manoeuvring?
retrieval_cards.why: This is the management-level mark. Anyone can recite the mechanism; the Class I candidate interrogates the claim.
